$$ P_{D}=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}:D\leq\lvert\{(a_{1},\dots,a_{k})\in A^{k}:a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}=z\}\rvert<2D\}. $$

Then:

$$ \displaystyle T_{k}(A) \displaystyle=\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}\lvert\{(a_{1},\dots,a_{k})\in A^{k}:a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}=z\}\rvert^{2} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}\left\lparen\sum_{D}2D\cdot\lvert\{(a,x)\in A\times P_{D}:a+x=z\}\rvert\right\rparen^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{D,D^{\prime}}\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}2D\cdot\lvert\{(a,x)\in A\times P_{D}:a+x=z\}\rvert\cdot 2D^{\prime}\cdot\lvert\{(a^{\prime},x^{\prime})\in A\times P_{D^{\prime}}:a^{\prime}+x^{\prime}=z\}\rvert\vphantom{\Bigg(^{2}} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{D,D^{\prime}}\left\lparen\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}4D^{2}\cdot\lvert\{(a,x)\in A\times P_{D}:a+x=z\}\rvert^{2}\right\rparen^{1/2} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\cdot\left\lparen\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}4(D^{\prime})^{2}\cdot\lvert\{(a^{\prime},x^{\prime})\in A\times P_{D^{\prime}}:a^{\prime}+x^{\prime}=z\}\rvert^{2}\right\rparen^{1/2} \displaystyle=\sum_{D,D^{\prime}}\left\lparen 4D^{2}\cdot E(A,P_{D})\right\rparen^{1/2}\left\lparen 4(D^{\prime})^{2}\cdot E(A,P_{D^{\prime}})\right\rparen^{1/2}. $$

We apply the dyadic pigeonhole principle: let $D$ denote the power of 2 maximizing $D^{2}\cdot E(A,P_{D})$ . Then:

$$ T_{k}(A)\leq O((k\log|A|)^{2})\cdot D^{2}\cdot E(A,P_{D}). $$

Recall that $T_{k}(A)\geq\Omega(|A|^{2k-1-c})$ by our initial assumption, and thus

$$ D^{2}\cdot E(A,P_{D})\geq|A|^{2k-1-c-o(1)}. $$

Combined with the trivial bounds $E(A,P_{D})\leq|A|^{2}|P_{D}|$ and $|P_{D}|\leq|A|^{k-1}/D$ , it further follows that $D\geq|A|^{k-2-c-o(1)}$ and thus $|P_{D}|\leq|A|^{1+c+o(1)}$ . Moreover, we have that

$$ |P_{D}|\cdot D^{2}\leq T_{k-1}(A)\leq|A|^{2(k-1)-1-c+\delta}. $$

Combining (2) and (3), it follows that

$$ E(A,P_{D})\geq\frac{|A|^{2}|P_{D}|}{|A|^{\delta+o(1)}}. $$

In this situation the asymmetric BSG theorem applies. Specifically, we apply Theorem 2.4 to the sets $A$ and $P_{D}$ with parameters $\epsilon^{\prime}=\epsilon/(4c)$ and $\alpha=|A|^{-\delta-o(1)}$ . It yields sets $H,\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that

$$ |H+H|\leq K|H|, $$

and

$$ |H|\leq|H|\,|\Lambda|\leq K|P_{D}|\leq(K|A|^{o(1)})\cdot|A|^{1+c}, $$

and

$$ |A\cap H|\geq\frac{|A|}{K}, $$

for some

$$ K\leq O_{\epsilon,c}\left\lparen\alpha^{-O_{\epsilon}(1)}\left\lparen 1+\frac{|P_{D}|}{|A|}\right\rparen^{\epsilon/(4c)}\right\rparen. $$

From the previous bounds on $K$ and $|P_{D}|/|A|$ , we can bound

$$ K\leq O_{\epsilon,c}(|A|^{O_{\epsilon,c}(\delta)+\epsilon/4+o(1)}). $$

Recall that $\delta=2c/k$ . Choose $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ sufficiently large so that this bound becomes $K\leq O_{\epsilon,c}(|A|^{\epsilon/2})$ . Then the right-hand side of (5) can be bounded by $O_{\epsilon,c}(|A|^{\epsilon})\cdot|A|^{1+c}$ . Hence, the set $H$ is as claimed by Equations 5, 4 and 6. ∎

### 3.3 Efficient Algorithm

We finally revisit the previous proof to demonstrate that all steps can be implemented efficiently, leading to the following algorithmic theorem:

#### 3.5.

For every $c>0$ and $\epsilon>0$ , there is some $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and some parameter $p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})$ , either certifies that $\Pop^{k}(A;p)=\emptyset$ , or otherwise computes a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that the following properties hold for some $K\leq O(|A|^{\epsilon})$ :

- • $|H|\leq K|A|^{1+c}$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ .

The algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon})$ .

The following lemma is analogous to Lemma 3.4.

#### 3.6.

For every $\epsilon,c>0$ , there is some $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that $T_{k}(A)\geq\Omega(|A|^{2k-1-c})$ computes a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that the following properties hold for some $K\leq O(|A|^{\epsilon})$ :

- • $|H|\leq K|A|^{1+c}$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ .

The algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon})$ .

We choose $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ as in Lemma 3.6. Given $A$ , we first apply Lemma 3.3 to compute a set $P$ satisfying (with high probability) that

$$ \Pop^{k}(A;p)\subseteq P\subseteq\Pop^{k}(A;p/2). $$

If $P=\emptyset$ , then we have certified that $\Pop^{k}(A;p)=\emptyset$ . So suppose otherwise that $P$ contains some element $z$ . We are guaranteed that $z$ is a $p/2$ -popular $k$ -sum in $A$ . We call Lemma 3.6 on the set $A^{*}=\pm(A\cup\{z\})$ with parameter $p/2$ . As before, it holds that $T_{k}(A^{*})\geq p/2$ and thus Lemma 3.6 computes a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ which is as claimed, except that instead of the third condition we have $|A^{*}\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ . However, as $A^{*}$ is a union of four copies of $A$ , possibly translated and negated, one of the corresponding translations and/or negations of $H$ must satisfy the claim. We test all four and verify each in linear time. The total time is dominated by the calls to Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6, running in time $\tilde{O}(|A|^{k}/p)=\tilde{O}(|A|^{1+c})$ and $O(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon})$ , respectively. ∎

Following the proof of Lemma 3.4, we design a recursive algorithm. If $T_{k}(A)$ is sufficiently large as in the lemma statement, then the algorithm returns $H$ satisfying the claimed properties with high probability. If the bound on $T_{k}(A)$ does not hold, then the algorithm may simply fail.

In the first case of the proof of Lemma 3.4, the set $A$ satisfies that $T_{k-1}(A)\geq|A|^{2(k-1)-1-c+\delta}$ , for some constant $\delta$ . Without knowing if this previous condition is actually satisfied, we regardless call the algorithm recursively for $k-1$ . If it reports $H$ as claimed, then we are done. Otherwise, we can infer that we instead in the second case.

In that second case, we construct sets $Q_{D}$ approximating the sets $P_{D}$ from the proof of Lemma 3.4 as follows. Here, $D$ ranges of all powers of $2$ at least $|A|^{k-1-c-o(1)}$ . Each set $Q_{D}$ is required to satisfy that (i) each $x\in Q_{D}$ has multiplicity at least $D/2$ and less than $4D$ as a $k$ -sum in $A$ and (ii) each $k$ -sum in $A$ with multiplicity at least $D$ and less than $2D$ is contained in $Q$ . Each such set $Q_{D}$ can be computed in time $\tilde{O}(|A|^{1+c})$ by a constant number of calls to Lemma 3.3. Then, by the same proof as in Lemma 3.4 we have that

$$ T_{k}(A)\leq O((k\log|A|)^{2})\cdot\max_{D}(D^{2}\cdot E(A,Q_{D})), $$

and thus

$$ E(A,Q_{D})\geq\frac{|A|^{2}|Q_{D}|}{|A|^{\delta+o(1)}} $$

for some choice of $D$ . In this case we apply the asymmetric BSG theorem on $A$ and $Q_{D}$ . In the algorithm, we do not know the optimal value of $D$ , so we simply try all $O(\log|A|)$ options. The algorithmic version of the asymmetric BSG theorem (Theorem 2.4) then returns the claimed set $H$ in time $\tilde{O}((|A|+|Q_{D}|)K)=O(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon+o(1)})$ . (The $o(1)$ overhead can be removed by reducing $\epsilon$ further.) ∎

## 4 Subquadratic-Time Algorithm for Low-Rank 3SUM

In this section we design a subquadratic-time algorithm for low-rank 3SUM.

#### 4.1Low-Rank 3SUM.

For every $0<\rho\leq 1/2$ there is some $\delta=\delta(\rho)>0$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that solves a given All-Integer 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ , when additionally provided with a set $X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ of size $|X|\leq n^{1-\rho}$ satisfying $A\subseteq X+X$ , and runs in time

$$ \ThreeSUM(n\mid r\leq n^{1-\rho})=O(n^{2-\delta}). $$

We will prove Theorem 4.1 by a sequence of two reduction steps to reduce from any given low-rank instance to few instances exhibiting even more structure. That structure is that the sets $A,B,C$ are all contained in some larger set $H$ with small doubling. For ease of notation we will typically refer to $H$ as a low-doubling container, formally defined as follows.

#### 4.2Low-Doubling Container.

We say that $H$ is a $(K,N)$ -container of some set $A$ if

- • $A\subseteq H$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ , and

- • $|H|\leq N$ .

Our reduction can then be phrased as follows:

#### 4.3From Low Rank to Low-Doubling Containment.

For every $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\rho\leq 1/2$ there is some $\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ and a set $X$ of size $|X|\leq n^{1-\rho}$ such that $C\subseteq X+X$ , computes

- • $O(n^{\epsilon})$ subinstances $(A^{\prime}\subseteq A,B^{\prime}\subseteq B,C^{\prime}\subseteq C)$ , each provided with a $(O(n^{\epsilon}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container of $A^{\prime}\cup B^{\prime}\cup C^{\prime}$ , and

- • a set of 3SUM solutions $\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C$ ,

so that each solution is either part of exactly one subinstance or part of $\mathcal{T}$ . The algorithm runs in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ .

We devote the following two subsections to the proof of Lemma 4.3. Once established, the proof of Theorem 4.1 is almost immediate by the following simple lemma.

#### 4.43SUM for Small Sumsets.

Any All-Integer 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ with universe $[u]$ can be solved in deterministic time $(|A+B|+|B-C|+|A-C|)(\log u)^{O(1)}$ .

To detect all elements in $C$ that are part of a solution, we compute the sumset $A+B$ by a sparse convolution in time $|A+B|(\log u)^{O(1)}$ by Lemma 2.2, and report all elements in $C\cap(A+B)$ . To detect all elements in $A$ and $B$ that are part of a solution, we proceed similarly with $A$ and $B$ in place of $C$ . ∎

Let $\epsilon>0$ be a parameter to be determined. We apply Lemma 4.3 to the given instance $(A,B,C)$ (by relabeling the input sets, we may assume $C$ has a low-doubling container as required by Lemma 4.3), and obtain $O(n^{\epsilon})$ subinstances $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},C^{\prime})$ and some set of 3SUM solutions $\mathcal{T}$ , with the promise that each solution in $(A,B,C)$ either appears in a subinstance or in $\mathcal{T}$ . We report all items present in $\mathcal{T}$ . Then we solve all subinstances by Lemma 4.4, and further report all items that appear in a solution in at least one subinstance. The correctness is clear.

It remains to analyze the running time. The call to Lemma 4.3 takes time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ for some constant $\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ . We can also charge the scan through $\mathcal{T}$ to that running time. By Lemma 4.3, each constructed subinstance $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},C^{\prime})$ admits an $(K=O(n^{\epsilon}),N=O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container $H$ of $A^{\prime}\cup B^{\prime}\cup C^{\prime}$ . It follows that

$$ |A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}|\leq|H+H|\leq K|H|\leq O(n^{2-2\rho+\epsilon}). $$

Similarly, by an application of the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality (Lemma 2.1),

$$ |B^{\prime}-C^{\prime}|\leq|H-H|\leq K^{2}|H|\leq O(n^{2-2\rho+2\epsilon}). $$

Therefore, the $O(n^{\epsilon})$ calls to Lemma 4.4 run in total time $O(n^{2-2\rho+3\epsilon})$ . The claimed running time follows, picking any constant $0<\epsilon<2\rho/3$ . ∎

### 4.1 Low-Doubling Containment for One Set

The proof of Lemma 4.3 involves two steps: (1) to reduce from any low-rank instance to subinstances where only one of the three sets admits a low-doubling container, and (2) to extend that one low-doubling container to all three sets. We start with step (1):

#### 4.5Low-Doubling Containment for One Set.

For every $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\rho\leq 1/2$ there is some $\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ and a set $X$ of size $|X|\leq n^{1-\rho}$ such that $C\subseteq X+X$ , computes

- • $O(n^{\epsilon})$ subinstances $(A^{\prime}\subseteq A,B,C)$ with $O(n^{\epsilon})$ -doubling $O(n^{2-2\rho})$ -containers of $A^{\prime}$ , and

- • a set of 3SUM solutions $\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C$ ,

so that each solution is either part of exactly one subinstance or part of $\mathcal{T}$ . The algorithm runs in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ .

The proof of Lemma 4.5 requires some setup. We start with the following simple lemma that allows to trade off the size of the container with its doubling.

#### 4.6.

Let $\epsilon,\gamma>0$ and $0<\rho\leq 1/2$ . There is a deterministic algorithm to reduce any 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ provided with a $(O(n^{\epsilon}),O(n^{2-2\rho+\gamma}))$ -container of $A$ to $O(n^{\gamma})$ subinstances $(A^{\prime}\subseteq A,B,C)$ provided with a $(O(n^{\epsilon+\gamma}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container of $A^{\prime}$ . It runs in linear time $O(n^{1+\gamma})$ .

Let $H$ denote the $K$ -doubling container of $A$ with $K=O(n^{\epsilon})$ . Arbitrarily partition $H$ into $t=O(n^{\gamma})$ pieces $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ of size at most $\lceil|H|/t\rceil=O(n^{2-2\rho})$ , and let $A_{1},\dots,A_{t}$ denote the subsets $A_{i}=A\cap H_{i}$ . Then the 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ is equivalent to the instances $(A_{1},B,C),\dots,(A_{t},B,C)$ (in the sense that their solutions stand in one-to-one correspondence). Moreover, each $A_{i}$ is contained in $H_{i}$ , and as

$$ |H_{i}+H_{i}|\leq|H+H|\leq K|H|\leq O(Kt)|H_{i}|=O(n^{\epsilon+\gamma})|H_{i}|, $$

$H_{i}$ is a $(O(n^{\epsilon+\gamma}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container of $A_{i}$ . ∎

The more interesting ingredient to Lemma 4.5 is the following lemma. Intuitively, it states that certain structure can be amplified. Namely, any 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ where $C$ is a subset of $(k+1)$ -popular sums can be replaced by a subinstance that is a subset of $(k+2)$ -popular sums. Curiously, the amplified structure does not show up in $C$ , but in $B$ .

#### 4.7.

There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ and integer parameters $p,s\geq 1$ and sets $X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ satisfying $C\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k};p)$ , computes

- • a subinstance $(A,B^{\prime}\subseteq B,C)$ so that $B^{\prime}\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k},-A;p^{\prime})$ for $p^{\prime}=p|A|/s$ , and

- • a set of 3SUM solutions $\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C$ ,

so that each solution is either part of the subinstance or part of $\mathcal{T}$ . The algorithm runs in time

$$ \widetilde{O}\left\lparen\frac{s|X|\,|Y_{1}|\dots|Y_{k}|}{p}+|A|\,|X|+\frac{|B|\,|Y_{1}|\dots|Y_{k}|}{p}+\frac{|A|\,|B|}{s}\right\rparen. $$

Let $p^{\prime}=p|A|/s$ . We run Lemma 3.3 to compute a set $P$ satisfying

$$ \Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k},-A;2p^{\prime})\subseteq P\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k},-A;p^{\prime}). $$

We call an item $b\in B$ popular if $b\in P$ and unpopular otherwise, and deal with the unpopular and popular items separately.

- • (Unpopular Items) Our strategy is to list all solutions $a+b=c$ involving an unpopular item $b$ . Let $Y\subseteq Y_{1}+\dots+Y_{k}$ be the set obtained by sampling some tuples $(y_{1},\dots,y_{k})\in Y_{1}\times\dots\times Y_{k}$ uniformly at random with rate $\min(1,R/p)$ for some $R=\Theta(\log n)$ ; for each such tuple we insert the sum $y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}$ into $Y$ . Then we run a meet-in-the-middle algorithm to explicitly list all solutions

$$ a+b=x+y $$

with $(a,b,x,y)\in A\times(B\setminus P)\times X\times Y$ . Note that this condition is equivalent to

$$ a-x=y-b, $$

an application of “Fredman’s trick” [37]. More specifically, enumerate all pairs $(a,x)\in A\times X$ , and store each pair in a hash table (with collision lists) indexed by $a-x$ . Then we enumerate all unpopular $b\in B\setminus P$ and all $y\in Y$ , and further list all entries $(a,x)$ in the hash table at index $y-b$ . For each 4-tuple $(a,b,x,y)$ listed in this way we test if $a+b\in C$ . We will show that this algorithm indeed lists any 3SUM solution involving an unpopular item.

- • (Popular Items) The only 3SUM solutions not listed in the previous step are those involving a popular item $b$ , i.e., the solutions of the subinstance $(A,B^{\prime},C)$ for $B^{\prime}=B\cap P$ . Recall that also $B^{\prime}\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k},-A;p^{\prime})$ by construction.

#### Correctness

We show that the first case of the algorithm indeed lists all solutions $a+b=c$ involving an unpopular item $b$ . From the initial assumption $C\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k};p)$ we get that $c$ can be expressed in at least $p$ ways as

$$ c=x+y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}, $$

for $x\in X$ and $y_{i}\in Y_{i}$ . Each such representation corresponds to a unique tuple $(y_{1},\dots,y_{k})$ (as each such tuple uniquely determines $x$ via $x=c-y_{1}-\dots-y_{k}$ ). By construction of $Y$ , with high probability $1-\exp(-O(R))=1-1/n^{\Omega(1)}$ , at least one such tuple $(y_{1},\dots,y_{k})$ is present in $Y$ in the form $y=y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}$ . In particular, $c$ can be expressed as $c=x+y$ for some $x\in X$ and $y\in Y$ , and therefore there is a solution $a+b=x+y$ . This solution is detected by the algorithm, and the correctness follows.

#### Running Time

The initial call to Lemma 3.3 takes time $\widetilde{O}(|X|\,|Y_{1}|\dots|Y_{k}|\,|A|/p^{\prime})$ . In the unpopular case, the construction of $Y$ takes time $O(|Y|)=O(|Y_{1}|\dots|Y_{k}|\cdot R/p)$ (which will turn out to be negligible). The meet-in-the-middle algorithm takes time $O(|A|\,|X|)$ to prepare the hash table, plus time $O(|B|\,|Y|)$ to enumerate all pairs $(a,x)$ . To bound the total time of listing all 4-tuples $(a,b,x,y)$ , note that each unpopular item $b$ can be represented in at most $2p^{\prime}$ ways as

$$ b=x+y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}-a. $$

For each such representation, the tuple $(y_{1},\dots,y_{k})$ is part of $Y$ only with probability $R/p$ , and thus the total number of solutions $a=x+y-b$ is at most $O(p^{\prime}\cdot R/p)=O(|A|/s\cdot R)$ (in expectation and with high probability) for any unpopular $b$ . In particular, the algorithm lists at most $O(|B|\,|A|/s\cdot R)$ such solutions overall. The popular case runs in linear time. ∎

We are finally ready to prove Lemma 4.5.

Let $c=1-2\rho+3\epsilon$ and let $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ be the constant from Theorem 3.5. Note that the statement of Lemma 4.3 allows us to arbitrarily decrease $\epsilon$ ; all parts of the lemma benefit from smaller $\epsilon$ , except for the non-explicit dependence of $\delta$ . For convenience we will therefore decrease $\epsilon$ whenever convenient.

#### Step 1: Removing Popular $k$ -Sums

We will first repeatedly remove elements from $A$ until it contains no more popular $k$ -sums/differences. More precisely, we will ensure that $\Pop^{k}(\pm A;p)=\emptyset$ for $p:=|A|^{k-1-c}$ .

Run Theorem 3.5 on $\pm A$ with parameter $p$ , leading to one of two possible outcomes. If it certifies that $\Pop^{k}(\pm A;p)=\emptyset$ , then step 1 is complete and we move on to step 2. Otherwise, Theorem 3.5 identifies a subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ of size $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/K$ along with a $K$ -doubling $K|A|^{2-2\rho+3\epsilon}$ -container of $A^{\prime}$ , for some $K=O(|A|^{\epsilon})$ . In this event we take $(A^{\prime},B,C)$ as one of the constructed subinstances (the container is not quite as claimed; we deal with this issue in a moment). We then remove $A^{\prime}$ from $A$ , and repeat the execution of step 1.

All in all, there can be at most $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{\epsilon})$ repetitions as each repetition removes $\Omega(|A|^{1-\epsilon})$ elements from $A$ . In particular, the number of constructed subinstances is $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{\epsilon})$ , and each subinstance is $O(|A|^{\epsilon})$ -doubling $O(|A|^{2-2\rho+4\epsilon})$ -contained. By Lemma 4.6 (applied with $t=|A|^{4\epsilon}$ ) we can further refine these subinstances to $O(|A|^{5\epsilon})$ instances that are $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{5\epsilon})$ -doubling $O(|A|^{2-2\rho})$ -contained. This is as claimed when reducing $\epsilon$ by a constant.

#### Step 2: Small Sets

Next, we easily assert that $n\leq|A|^{1+\epsilon}$ . Otherwise we can solve the whole instance trivially in time $n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon)}$ , and report the set of solutions $\mathcal{T}$ .

#### Step 3: Popular $k$ -Sum Covers

Once we reach this step, we will exhaustively list all 3SUM solutions. Let $\mathcal{T}$ be initially empty. We will successively remove elements from $B$ and $C$ , while maintaining the invariant that each 3SUM solution that is eliminated in this way has already been listed in $\mathcal{T}$ . The algorithm runs in iterations $\ell=1,\dots,k$ . We also maintain the second invariant that, before the $\ell$ -th iteration,

$$ \begin{cases}B\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\ell};p_{\ell})&\text{if $\ell$ is even,}\\
C\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\ell};p_{\ell})&\text{if $\ell$ is odd.}\end{cases} $$

To satisfy this invariant initially (for $\ell=1$ ) we pick $Y_{1}=X$ and $p_{1}=1$ ; indeed, then the invariant follows from the assumption $C\subseteq X+X$ . Let $s=|A|^{\epsilon/k}$ . Each iteration depends on the parity of $\ell$ :

- • If $\ell$ is odd: Apply Lemma 4.7 on the 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ , with parameters $p_{\ell}$ and $s$ and sets $X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\ell}$ ; the invariant makes sure that the premise $C\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\ell};p_{\ell})$ is fulfilled. This yields a set of solutions $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ and a subinstance $(A,B^{\prime}\subseteq B,C)$ . We update: $\displaystyle\mathcal{T}$ $\displaystyle:=\mathcal{T}\cup\mathcal{T}^{\prime},$ $\displaystyle B$ $\displaystyle:=B^{\prime},$ $\displaystyle Y_{\ell+1}$ $\displaystyle:=-A,$ $\displaystyle p_{\ell+1}$ $\displaystyle:=\frac{p_{\ell}|A|}{s}.$ Lemma 4.7 states that each 3SUM solution is either in $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ or part of the instance $(A,B^{\prime},C)$ . Thus, after the update each solution is either in $\mathcal{T}$ or part of the instance $(A,B,C)$ , and therefore the first invariant is maintained. Lemma 4.7 also guarantees that $B^{\prime}\subseteq\Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\ell},-A;p_{\ell}|A|/s)$ . After the update, this precisely maintains the second invariant.

- • If $\ell$ is even: Observe that our 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ is equivalent to the appropriately transposed instance $(A,-C,-B)$ , i.e., their solutions stand in one-to-one correspondence. Apply Lemma 4.7 on $(A,-C,-B)$ with parameters $p_{\ell}$ and $s$ and sets $-X,-Y_{1},\dots,-Y_{\ell}$ ; the premise $-B\subseteq\Pop(-X,-Y_{1},\dots,-Y_{\ell};p_{\ell})$ is satisfied by our invariant. This yields a set of solutions $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ and a subinstance $(A,C^{\prime}\subseteq-C,-B)$ . We update: $\displaystyle\mathcal{T}$ $\displaystyle:=\mathcal{T}\cup\{(a,b,c):(a,-c,-b)\in\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\},$ $\displaystyle C$ $\displaystyle:=-C^{\prime},$ $\displaystyle Y_{\ell+1}$ $\displaystyle:=A,$ $\displaystyle p_{\ell+1}$ $\displaystyle:=\frac{p_{\ell}|A|}{s}.$ Similarly to before, Lemma 4.7 states that each transposed 3SUM solution is either in $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ or part of the instance $(A,C^{\prime},-B)$ . Thus, after the update each original solution is either in $\mathcal{T}$ or part of the instance $(A,B,C)$ , and therefore the first invariant is maintained. Lemma 4.7 also guarantees that $C^{\prime}\subseteq\Pop(-X,-Y_{1},\dots,-Y_{\ell},-A;p_{\ell}|A|/s)$ . After the update, this precisely maintains the second invariant.

Once the final $k$ -th iteration is complete, we report the set $\mathcal{T}$ and the subinstances constructed in step 1. This completes the description of the algorithm.

#### Correctness

The correctness of steps 1 and 2 is fairly obvious; the interesting part is to argue that in step 3 we exhaustively list all solutions of $(A,B,C)$ . The key correctness claim is that once the $k$ -th iteration terminates, $B$ or $C$ must be empty. Suppose otherwise that both are non-empty. Then our invariant implies that

$$ \Pop(X,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1};p_{k+1})\neq\emptyset. $$

Recall that we picked $p_{1}=1$ and $p_{\ell+1}=p_{\ell}|A|/s$ , and thus

$$ p_{k+1}=\frac{|A|^{k}}{s^{k}}. $$

Moreover, we picked $Y_{1}=X$ and $Y_{2},\dots,Y_{k+1}\subseteq\pm A$ . In combination, we get

$$ \Pop\bigg(X,X,\underbrace{\pm A,\dots,\pm A}_{\text{$k$ times}};\frac{|A|^{k}}{s^{k}}\bigg)\neq\emptyset. $$

By two applications of Observation 3.2 it further follows that

$$ \Pop^{k}\left\lparen\pm A;\frac{|A|^{k}}{|X|^{2}s^{k}}\right\rparen\neq\emptyset. $$

But note that

$$ \frac{|A|^{k}}{|X|^{2}s^{k}}\geq\frac{|A|^{k}}{n^{2-2\rho}|A|^{\epsilon}}\geq\frac{|A|^{k}}{|A|^{2-2\rho+2\epsilon}|A|^{\epsilon}}=|A|^{k-2+2\rho-3\epsilon}=|A|^{k-1-c}=p, $$

where we used that $|X|\leq n^{1-\rho}$ and that $n\leq|A|^{1+\epsilon}$ as asserted in step 2. Hence,

$$ \Pop^{k}(\pm A;p)\neq\emptyset, $$

which contradicts step 1.

#### Running Time

The running time of step 1 is dominated by the calls to Theorem 3.5, running in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon})=\widetilde{O}(|A|^{2-2\rho+4\epsilon})$ for each call, and in total $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{2-2\rho+5\epsilon})$ over all $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{\epsilon})$ calls. Step 2 runs in time $O(n^{2-\delta_{0}})$ for some constant $\delta_{0}=\delta_{0}(\epsilon)>0$ . Finally, focus on step 3. For $1\leq\ell\leq k$ , the $\ell$ -th iteration is dominated by the call to Lemma 4.7. In the odd case, this takes time

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{O}\left\lparen\frac{s|X|\,|Y_{1}|\dots|Y_{\ell}|}{p_{\ell}}+|A|\,|X|+\frac{|B|\,|Y_{1}|\dots|Y_{\ell}|}{p_{\ell}}+\frac{|A|\,|B|}{s}\right\rparen \displaystyle\qquad{}=\widetilde{O}\left\lparen\frac{s^{\ell}|X|^{2}|A|^{\ell-1}}{|A|^{\ell-1}}+|A|\,|X|+\frac{s^{\ell-1}|B|\,|X|\,|A|^{\ell-1}}{|A|^{\ell-1}}+\frac{|A|\,|B|}{s}\right\rparen \displaystyle\qquad{}=\widetilde{O}\left\lparen n^{2-2\rho+\epsilon\ell/k}+n^{2-\rho}+n^{2-\rho+\epsilon(\ell-1)/k}+n^{2-\epsilon/k}\right\rparen, $$

and the running time of the even case can be bounded analogously. Note that the fourth term can be bounded by $O(n^{2-\delta_{1}})$ for some constant $\delta_{1}=\delta_{1}(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ . This leaves the first three terms, and the time complexity of step 1, which are crudely bounded by $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\rho+5\epsilon})$ . If necessary, decrease $\epsilon$ further so that $\epsilon<\rho/10$ . Then let $\delta=\min(\delta_{0},\delta_{1},\rho/2)$ , and the proof is complete. ∎

### 4.2 Low-Doubling Containment for All Sets

Next, we demonstrate that low-doubling containment for one set can be extended to low-doubling containment for all three sets:

#### 4.8Low-Doubling Containment for All Sets.

Let $\epsilon>0$ . There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ along with a $(K,N)$ -container $H$ of $A$ , computes

- • $O(n^{\epsilon})$ subinstances $(A,B^{\prime}\subseteq B,C^{\prime}\subseteq C)$ so that $B^{\prime}$ is contained in a translate of $H$ and $C^{\prime}$ is contained in a translate of $H+H$ , and

- • a set of 3SUM solutions $\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C$ ,

so that each solution is either part of exactly one subinstance or part of $\mathcal{T}$ . The algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(KNn^{\epsilon}+Kn^{2-\epsilon})$ .

The proof closely follows Jin and Xu’s algorithm for low-doubling 3SUM [40, Section 3.3]. The key ingredient is the following covering-type lemma [40].

#### 4.9[40, Lemma 3.6].

There is a randomized algorithm that, given integer sets $H,B,C$ of size at most $N$ with $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ , computes subsets $B_{1},\dots,B_{m}\subseteq B$ and $C_{1},\dots,C_{m}\subseteq C$ such that:

- (i) $B_{1},\dots,B_{m}$ form a partition of $B$ ,

- (ii) $\sum_{i}|C_{i}|\leq O(|C|K\log N)$ ,

- (iii) for all $1\leq i\leq m$ , there is a translate $s_{i}$ so that $B_{i}\subseteq(s_{i}+H)\cap B$ and $C_{i}=(s_{i}+H+H)\cap C$ .

The algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(NK\log u)$ whenever $H,B,C\subseteq[-u,u]$ .

The sets $H,B,C$ satisfy the premise of Lemma 4.9, yielding sets $B_{1},\dots,B_{m}$ and $C_{1},\dots,C_{m}$ . By Properties 1 and 3 and the fact that $A\subseteq H$ , each 3SUM solution from $(A,B,C)$ must be contained in a subinstance $(A,B_{i},C_{i})$ .

Consider all such subinstances, distinguishing two cases. If $|B_{i}|\leq|B|^{1-\epsilon}$ , we simply solve the subinstance by brute-force in time $O(|B_{i}|\,|C_{i}|)=O(|B|^{1-\epsilon}\,|C_{i}|)$ . Otherwise, we keep it as one of the designated subinstances. Property 3 guarantees that $B_{i}$ is contained in a translate of $H$ and $C_{i}$ is a translate of $H+H$ , as claimed. Moreover, we designate at most $|B|^{\epsilon}$ subinstances in total, recalling that the sets $B_{1},\dots,B_{m}$ form a partition of $B$ by Property 1. This completes the description of the algorithm. The correctness is immediate.

We focus on the running time. The initial call to Lemma 4.9 takes time $\widetilde{O}(NK\log u)$ where $N$ is the maximum size of $H,B,C$ . Solving the subinstance $(A,B_{i},C_{i})$ takes time $\widetilde{O}(|B|^{1-\epsilon}\,|C_{i}|)$ by brute-force, or linear time to copy the instance to the set of reported instances. Therefore, the total time across all subinstances is

$$ O\left\lparen\sum_{i=1}^{m}|B|^{1-\epsilon}\,|C_{i}|+n^{1+\epsilon}\right\rparen=\widetilde{O}\lparen|B|^{1-\epsilon}\cdot K|C|+n^{1+\epsilon}\rparen=\widetilde{O}(Kn^{2-\epsilon}+n^{1+\epsilon}), $$

by Property 2. Hence, the total time of the algorithm is

$$ \widetilde{O}(NK+Kn^{2-\epsilon}+n^{1+\epsilon})=\widetilde{O}(KNn^{\epsilon}+Kn^{2-\epsilon}) $$

as claimed. ∎

Finally, the proof of Lemma 4.3 is now a simple combination of Lemmas 4.5 and 4.8.

We start from a 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ where $C$ has rank at most $n^{1-\rho}$ . Let $\epsilon_{1}=\frac{\epsilon}{4}$ and $\epsilon_{2}=\frac{3\epsilon}{4}$ . Lemma 4.5 reduces this instance to $O(n^{\epsilon_{1}})$ subinstances $(A^{\prime}\subseteq A,B,C)$ , each provided with a $(K=O(n^{\epsilon_{1}}),N=O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container $H$ of $A^{\prime}$ . We pass each such instance to Lemma 4.8, obtaining $O(n^{\epsilon_{2}})$ subinstances $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\subseteq B,C^{\prime}\subseteq C)$ where $B^{\prime}$ is covered by a translate of $H$ and $C^{\prime}$ is covered by a translate of $H+H$ . Pick

$$ H^{\prime}=H\cup B^{\prime}\cup C^{\prime}; $$

we claim that this is a $(O(K^{4}),O(N))$ -container of $A^{\prime}\cup B^{\prime}\cup C^{\prime}$ . The containment condition is clear, and the size of $H^{\prime}$ is bounded by $|H|+|B|+|C|\leq N+2n\leq O(N)$ . Regarding the doubling of $H^{\prime}$ , observe that $H^{\prime}+H^{\prime}$ can be covered by $O(1)$ translates of $H+H+H+H$ . Thus, by the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality (Lemma 2.1),

$$ |H^{\prime}+H^{\prime}|\leq O(|H+H+H+H|)\leq O(K^{4})|H|\leq O(K^{4})|H^{\prime}|. $$

In summary, it follows that $H^{\prime}$ is indeed a $(O(n^{4\epsilon_{1}})=O(n^{\epsilon}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container of $A^{\prime}\cup B^{\prime}\cup C^{\prime}$ . Moreover, the total number of instances is $O(n^{\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2}})=O(n^{\epsilon})$ .

Let us finally analyze the running time. The reduction in Lemma 4.5 takes time $O(n^{2-\delta_{1}})$ for some constant $\delta_{1}=\delta_{1}(\rho,\epsilon_{1})>0$ . Each of the $O(n^{\epsilon_{1}})$ calls to Lemma 4.8 takes time $\widetilde{O}(KNn^{\epsilon_{2}}+Kn^{2-\epsilon_{2}})$ , amounting to a total time of

$$ \widetilde{O}(n^{\epsilon_{1}}\cdot(KNn^{\epsilon_{2}}+Kn^{2-\epsilon_{2}}))=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2\rho+2\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2}}+n^{2+2\epsilon_{1}-\epsilon_{2}})=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2\rho+5\epsilon/4}+n^{2-\epsilon/4}). $$

If necessary, decrease $\epsilon$ to $4\rho/5$ so that the first term becomes $O(n^{2-\rho})$ . Then the running time is as claimed for any constant $0<\delta<\min(\delta_{1},\rho,\frac{\epsilon}{4})$ . ∎

## 5 Universe Reductions for Min-Plus Convolution

In this section we design our universe reductions for Min-Plus Convolution. These work somewhat differently in two regimes, and thus we design a “small-universe reduction” from $[n]$ to $[n^{\gamma}]$ , for $\gamma<1$ , and a separate “large-universe reduction” from $[n^{c}]$ to $[n]$ , for $c>1$ . We start with the simpler small-universe reduction in Section 5.1. Then, to prepare the more involved large-universe reduction, in Section 5.2 we first design a “doubling reduction”, proving that the index sets of the given sequences can be assumed to have low-doubling containers. In Section 5.3 we then design a universe reduction for the Monotone Min-Plus Convolution problem. Finally, in Section 5.4 we put these two pieces together to obtain the large-universe reduction, conditioned on Hypothesis 1.7.

### 5.1 Small-Universe Reduction

The small-universe reduction can be stated as follows:

#### 5.1Small-Universe Reduction.

For any $0\leq\gamma\leq 1$ and $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \MinPlusConv(n\mid u\leq n)=\widetilde{O}\left\lparen n^{\epsilon}\cdot\MinPlusConvListing(n,n^{1-\gamma}\mid u\leq n^{\gamma})+\ThreeSUM(n\mid r\leq n^{1-\epsilon/2})\right\rparen. $$

Let $(A,B)$ be the given Min-Plus Convolution instance with universe $[0,n]$ . Let $q=\lceil n^{1-\gamma}\rceil$ , and rewrite these sequences as

$$ \displaystyle A \displaystyle=A_{1}\cdot q+A_{0}, \displaystyle B \displaystyle=B_{1}\cdot q+B_{0}, $$

where $A_{1},B_{1}$ have entries less than $n/q\leq n^{\gamma}$ (or $\bot$ ), and $A_{0},B_{0}$ have entries less than $q$ (or $\bot$ ). In fact, we may assume without loss of generality that $A_{0},B_{0}$ have entries bounded by $q/2$ (or $\bot$ ). Indeed, simply split $A_{0}$ into two subsequences, retaining in one the entries less than $q/2$ and in the other the remaining entries. From the second one subtract $q/2$ globally. This leaves two subproblems for which $A_{0}$ is as claimed. Proceeding similarly with $B_{0}$ yields at most four subinstances for which $A_{0},B_{0}$ have entries less than $q/2$ .

We compute $C_{1}=A_{1}*B_{1}$ in time $O(\MinPlusConv(n\mid u\leq n^{\gamma}))$ (which is dominated by the first term in Equation 7). As $A_{0},B_{0}$ have entries less than $q/2$ , we know that

$$ C[k]=C_{1}[k]\cdot q+C_{0}[k], $$

where

$$ C_{0}[k]=\min\{A_{0}[i]+B_{0}[k-i]:i\in[0,n],\,A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[k-i]=C_{1}[k]\}, $$

so the remaining task is to compute $C_{0}[k]$ .

In fact, we can learn a close approximation of $C_{0}[k]$ by a simple scaling trick. Let $A_{0}^{\prime}=\lfloor A_{0}/2\rfloor$ and $B_{0}^{\prime}=\lfloor B_{0}/2\rfloor$ (applied coordinate-wise), and recursively compute

$$ C_{0}^{\prime}[k]=\min\{A_{0}^{\prime}[i]+B_{0}^{\prime}[k-i]:i\in[0,n],\,A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[k-i]=C_{1}[k]\}. $$

It is easy to check that $2C_{0}^{\prime}[k]\leq C_{0}[k]\leq 2C_{0}^{\prime}[k]+2$ , leaving only three candidates for each $C[k]$ . In what follows we will determine the correct choice among these three candidates.

We call an index $i$ satisfying $A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[k-i]=C_{1}[k]$ a pseudo-witness of $k$ . We say that $k$ is popular if it has at least $n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon}$ pseudo-witnesses, and unpopular otherwise. We will compute the value of $C[k]$ by one of the two following algorithms, depending on whether $k$ is popular or unpopular.

- • (Unpopular) We first show how to compute $(A*B)[k]$ for all unpopular indices $k$ . For any such $k$ , we can afford to list all $n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon}$ pseudo-witnesses, then compute $C_{0}[k]$ and $C[k]$ via the previous identities. This takes time

$$ O\lparen\MinPlusConvListing(n,n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon}\mid u\leq n^{\gamma})\rparen=O\lparen n^{\epsilon}\cdot\MinPlusConvListing(n,n^{1-\gamma}\mid u\leq n^{\gamma})\rparen, $$

by Lemma 2.14, which constitutes the first term in Equation 7.

- • (Popular) It remains to compute $C[k]$ for all popular indices $k$ . Let $X\subseteq[0,n]$ be a random subset including each index independently with probability $p=\sqrt{(100\log n)/n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon}}$ . Then let $\displaystyle\mathcal{X}_{1}$ $\displaystyle=\{(i,A_{1}[i]\cdot q+a):i\in X,\,0\leq a<\lceil\sqrt{q}\rceil\},$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{X}_{2}$ $\displaystyle=\{(j,B_{1}[j]\cdot q+b\cdot\lceil\sqrt{q}\rceil):j\in X,\,0\leq b<\lceil\sqrt{q}\rceil\},$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{X}$ $\displaystyle=\mathcal{X}_{1}\cup\mathcal{X}_{2}.$ Consider the All-Integer 3SUM instance $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})$ on the following index sets $\displaystyle\mathcal{A}$ $\displaystyle=\{(i,A[i]):i\in[0,n]\},$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{B}$ $\displaystyle=\{(j,B[j]):j\in[0,n]\},$ $\displaystyle\mathcal{C}$ $\displaystyle=\{(k,C_{1}[k]\cdot q+2C_{0}^{\prime}[k]+z):k\in[0,2n],\ z\in\{0,1,2\}\}\cap(\mathcal{X}_{1}+\mathcal{X}_{2}).$ By construction, $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{1}+\mathcal{X}_{2}$ and thus $\mathcal{C}$ has rank at most

$$ r:=\max\{|\mathcal{X}_{1}|,|\mathcal{X}_{2}|\}\leq O(|X|\sqrt{q})\leq O(pn\cdot\sqrt{q})=\widetilde{O}(n^{1-\epsilon/2}), $$

where $|X|\leq 2pn$ follows from Chernoff’s bound with high probability. We solve the All-Integer 3SUM instance in time

$$ \widetilde{O}(\ThreeSUM(n\mid r\leq n^{1-\epsilon/2})), $$

constituting the second term in the claimed running time. For each $k$ , choose the smallest of the three items $(k,c)\in\mathcal{C}$ that is involved in a 3SUM solution, and set $C[k]=c$ . We argue that we thereby correctly assign $C[k]$ for all popular indices $k$ . By definition, a popular index has at least $n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon}$ pseudo-witnesses $i$ . Thus, with good probability $X$ contains one such pseudo-witness $i$ and simultaneously $k-i$ ; the probability of missing all such pairs is

$$ (1-p^{2})^{n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon}}\leq\exp(-p^{2}n^{1-\gamma+\epsilon})\leq n^{-100}. $$

In the successful event, we have $(i,A_{1}[i]\cdot q+a)\in\mathcal{X}_{1}$ and $(j,B_{1}[j]\cdot q+b\cdot\lceil\sqrt{q}\rceil)\in\mathcal{X}_{2}$ for all $0\leq a,b<\sqrt{q}$ , and thus $(k,C_{1}[k]\cdot q+a+b\cdot\lceil\sqrt{q}\rceil)\in\mathcal{X}_{1}+\mathcal{X}_{2}$ . For an appropriate choice of $0\leq a,b<\sqrt{q}$ , this becomes exactly $(k,C_{1}[k]\cdot q+C_{0}[k])=(k,C[k])$ . In this event, $(k,C[k])$ is part of the All-Integer 3SUM instance and we correctly identify $C[k]$ . ∎

#### 5.2Small-Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution Listing.

Let $\gamma\in[0,1]$ . Listing $n^{1-\gamma}$ witnesses in Min-Plus Convolution instances with universe $[n^{\gamma}]$ requires $n^{2-o(1)}$ time, under the strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis.

Suppose there is such an algorithm with running time $O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}})$ . We invoke Lemma 5.1 with $\gamma:=\gamma$ and $\epsilon=\epsilon^{\prime}/2$ . Combined with Theorem 4.1, this gives us a truly subquadratic time algorithm for $\MinPlusConv(n\mid u\leq n)$ , contradicting the strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis. ∎

### 5.2 Doubling Reduction

The purpose of this subsection is to prove the following lemma. Intuitively, it states that any Min-Plus Convolution instance $(A,B)$ can be assumed to have a low-doubling container for its joint index set $\mathcal{I}(A)\cup\mathcal{I}(B)$ (Definition 2.13). The proof is close to [36, Lemma 5.7].

#### 5.3Doubling Reduction.

For any $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\rho\leq 1/2$ there is some $\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized reduction from any Min-Plus Convolution instance $(A,B)$ over the universe $[u]$ to $O(n^{\epsilon}\log u)$ Min-Plus Convolution Listing instances $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime})$ with the same size $n$ , over the same universe $[u]$ , and with listing threshold $O(n^{2\rho})$ , each equipped with a $(O(n^{\epsilon}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container of the joint index set $\mathcal{I}(A^{\prime})\cup\mathcal{I}(B^{\prime})$ . The reduction runs in time $O((n^{1+2\rho+\epsilon}+n^{2-\delta})\log u)$ .

Let $(A,B)$ denote the given Min-Plus Convolution instance; each entry of $A$ and $B$ is either an integer in $[u]$ or $\bot$ (viewed as $+\infty$ ). We call $i\in[0,n]$ a witness of $(A*B)[k]$ if $A[i]+B[k-i]=(A*B)[k]$ , and a $q$ -pseudo-witness if $A[i]+B[k-i]<(A*B)[k]+q$ . Let $L=\lceil\log(2u)\rceil$ and let $t=100\lceil n^{2\rho}\rceil$ . We classify the indices $k$ into three different kinds, based on their number of pseudo-witnesses:

- 1. $k$ is exceptionally popular if $(A*B)[k]$ has at least $t$ $1$ -pseudo-witnesses (i.e., witnesses),

- 2. $k$ is exceptionally unpopular if $(A*B)[k]$ has at most $t$ $2^{L}$ -pseudo-witnesses,

- 3. and otherwise $k$ is ordinary. In this case, there is some scale $0\leq\ell<L$ such that $(A*B)[k]$ has at most $t$ $2^{\ell}$ -pseudo-witnesses, and simultaneously at least $t$ $2^{\ell+1}$ -pseudo-witnesses. We say that $(A*B)[k]$ is relevant at that scale $\ell$ .

The reduction deals with the exceptionally popular, exceptionally unpopular, and ordinary pairs in three different cases (though we never have to explicitly determine which index falls into which case). Out of these only the third one is interesting; the others are corner cases. Throughout we maintain a sequence $C$ initialized to $\bot$ . We will only ever modify $C$ via updates of the form $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[k-i]\}$ , ensuring that we never underestimate the convolution.

- 1. (Exceptionally Popular) Repeat the following $N=\lceil n^{2-2\rho}\cdot 100\log n\rceil$ times: Randomly sample $i,j\in[0,n]$ , and update $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[j]\}$ for $k=i+j$ . We argue that, afterwards, $C[k]$ is correctly assigned for each exceptionally popular index $k$ . Indeed, for any such index the probability of missing all pairs $(i,k-i)$ where $i$ is a witness of $k$ is at most

$$ \left\lparen 1-\frac{t}{n^{2}}\right\rparen^{N}\leq\exp\left\lparen-\frac{tN}{n^{2}}\right\rparen\leq\frac{1}{n^{100}}. $$

Thus, with high probability we list one such pair and consequently assign $C[k]=(A*B)[k]$ .

- 2. (Exceptionally Unpopular) By definition, a $2^{L}$ -pseudo-witness $i$ of $(A*B)[k]$ is any index satisfying that $A[i]\neq\bot$ and $B[k-i]\neq\bot$ . Thus, to list the at most $t$ $2^{L}$ -pseudo-witnesses of the exceptionally unpopular indices $k$ , we can simply construct the sequences $A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\in\{0,\bot\}^{[0,n]}$ obtained from $A,B$ by replacing any non- $\bot$ entry by $0$ , and then for each exceptionally unpopular index we can directly list $t$ witnesses of a Boolean convolution (Lemma 2.15), running in time $\widetilde{O}(tn)=\widetilde{O}(n^{1+2\rho})$ . The output is a set of witnesses, i.e., triples $(i,j,k)$ with $A^{\prime}[i]+B^{\prime}[j]=(A^{\prime}*B^{\prime})[k]$ , or equivalently, $A[i]\neq\bot$ and $B[j]\neq\bot$ . For each such triple update $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[j]\}$ .

- 3. (Ordinary) For all $0\leq\ell<L$ , all $x,y\in\{0,1\}$ and all $z\in[-4,4]$ , repeat the following steps $100\log n$ times: 3.1. Construct the sequences $P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ by $\displaystyle P[i]$ $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle{\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle{\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle{\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor}$\hss}}\phantom{\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor}&\text{if $(A[i]\bmod 2^{\ell})\in x2^{\ell-1}+[0,2^{\ell-1})$,}\\ \bot&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$ $\displaystyle Q[j]$ $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor&\text{if $(B[j]\bmod 2^{\ell})\in y2^{\ell-1}+[0,2^{\ell-1})$,}\\ \bot&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ Sample $X\subseteq[0,n]$ uniformly at random with rate $p=n^{-\rho}$ . By Chernoff’s bound, this set has size $|X|=O(n^{1-\rho})$ with high probability. Compute the sequence $R\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}$ defined by

$$ R[k]=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in X\\ i+j=k\end{subarray}}\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+z $$

by brute-force. Moreover, construct the set

$$ \mathcal{X}=\left\{\left\lparen i,\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor\right\rparen:i\in X\right\}\cup\left\{\left\lparen j,\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+z\right\rparen:j\in X\right\}, $$

and observe that $\mathcal{R}:=\mathcal{I}(R)\subseteq\mathcal{X}+\mathcal{X}$ . In particular, the rank of $\mathcal{R}$ is at most $r=|\mathcal{X}|\leq 2|X|=O(n^{1-\rho})$ . 3.2. For convenience, write $\mathcal{P}:=\mathcal{I}(P)$ and $\mathcal{Q}:=\mathcal{I}(Q)$ . Apply Lemma 4.3 to the 3SUM instance $(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R})$ and the set $\mathcal{X}$ (which satisfies $\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{X}+\mathcal{X}$ , as required). This is an instance of 3SUM over the group $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , which can be easily mapped to plain integers via the standard embedding into disjoint bit-blocks. The output of Lemma 4.3 consists of • $O(n^{\epsilon})$ subinstances $(\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{R})$ , each provided with a $(O(n^{\epsilon}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$ , and • a set of 3SUM solutions $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{Q}\times\mathcal{R}$ . 3.3. For each triple $((i,a),(j,b),(k,c))\in\mathcal{T}$ : Update $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[j]\}$ . 3.4. For each subinstance $(\mathcal{P}^{\prime},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime},\mathcal{R}^{\prime})$ : Let $P^{\prime}$ denote the restriction of $P$ so that $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\mathcal{I}(P^{\prime})$ . Similarly, let $Q^{\prime}$ denote the restriction of $Q$ so that $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}=\mathcal{I}(Q^{\prime})$ . Let $(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})$ be one of the designated Min-Plus Convolution Listing instances with threshold $t$ . We solve the instance by the reduction. The output is a set of witnesses, i.e., triples $(i,j,k)$ with $P^{\prime}[i]+Q^{\prime}[j]=(P^{\prime}*Q^{\prime})[k]$ . For each such triple update $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[j]\}$ .

In the end, we return the sequence $C$ computed before. This completes the description of the algorithm. It should be clear that cases 1 and 2 correctly assign $C[k]=(A*B)[k]$ for all exceptional indices $k$ , but it remains to show that the same holds for the ordinary ones.

Fix any ordinary index $k^{*}$ . Let $0\leq\ell<L$ be the scale at which $k^{*}$ becomes relevant (i.e., $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ has at most $t$ $2^{\ell}$ -pseudo-witnesses and at least $t$ $2^{\ell+1}$ -pseudo-witnesses). Also, fix any witness $i^{*}$ of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ and let $j^{*}=k^{*}-i^{*}$ . Let $x,y\in\{0,1\}$ be such that $(A[i^{*}]\bmod 2^{\ell})\in x2^{\ell-1}+[0,2^{\ell-1})$ and $(B[j^{*}]\bmod 2^{\ell})\in y2^{\ell-1}+[0,2^{\ell-1})$ . Now focus on any iteration corresponding to our choice of $\ell,x,y$ (and some $z$ to be determined soon).

#### 5.4.

In any iteration corresponding to these choices of $\ell,x,y$ , it holds that:

- (i) $i^{*}$ is a witness of $(P*Q)[k^{*}]$ , and $P[i^{*}]+Q[j^{*}]\leq\lfloor(A*B)[k^{*}]/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ , and

- (ii) every witness of $(P*Q)[k^{*}]$ is a $2^{\ell}$ -pseudo-witness of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ .

By definition, $P$ is only supported on the indices $i$ with $(A[i]\bmod 2^{\ell})\in x2^{\ell-1}+[0,2^{\ell-1})$ and analogously, $Q$ is only supported on the indices $j$ with $(B[j]\bmod 2^{\ell})\in y2^{\ell-1}+[0,2^{\ell-1})$ . Let $i,j$ be two indices satisfying these requirements. Then:

$$ P[i]+Q[j]=\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor=\frac{A[i]+B[j]-(A[i]\bmod 2^{\ell})-(B[j]\bmod 2^{\ell})}{2^{\ell}}. $$

This can be upper bounded by

$$ P[i]+Q[j]\leq\frac{A[i]+B[j]-(x+y)2^{\ell-1}}{2^{\ell}}, $$

and correspondingly lower bounded by

$$ P[i]+Q[j]>\frac{A[i]+B[j]-(x+y)2^{\ell-1}-2^{\ell}}{2^{\ell}}=\frac{A[i]+B[j]-(x+y)2^{\ell-1}}{2^{\ell}}-1. $$

But as this is an integer, we must have

$$ P[i]+Q[j]=\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]+B[j]-(x+y)2^{\ell-1}}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor. $$

Hence, since $x,y,\ell$ are fixed, it is minimized for any witness $(A*B)[i+j]$ . In particular, $i^{*}$ is a witness of $(P*Q)[k^{*}]$ , and

$$ P[i^{*}]+Q[j^{*}]=\left\lfloor\frac{(A*B)[k^{*}]-(x+y)2^{\ell-1}}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor\leq\left\lfloor\frac{(A*B)[k^{*}]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor, $$

proving 1. Moreover, for any witness $i$ of $(P*Q)[k^{*}]$ , $A[i]+B[k^{*}-i]$ cannot differ from $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ by $2^{\ell}$ or more, proving 2. ∎

#### 5.5.

There is some $z\in[-4,4]$ such that, in any iteration corresponding to these choices of $\ell,x,y,z$ , with probability at least $0.9$ it holds that $P[i^{*}]+Q[j^{*}]=R[k^{*}]$ .

We derive lower and upper bounds on

$$ \min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in X\\
i+j=k^{*}\end{subarray}}\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor. $$

On the one hand, a simple lower bound is $\lfloor(A*B)[k^{*}]/2^{\ell}\rfloor-2$ . On the other hand, $X$ contains some $2^{\ell+1}$ -pseudo-witness $i^{\prime}$ of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ with probability at least $1-(1-p^{2})^{t}\geq 1-\exp(-p^{2}t)=1-\exp(-n^{-2\rho}\cdot 100\lceil n^{2\rho}\rceil)\geq 0.9$ . Conditioned on this event, we have

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in X\\
i+j=k^{*}\end{subarray}}\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor \displaystyle\leq\left\lfloor\frac{A[i^{\prime}]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{B[k^{*}-i^{\prime}]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor \displaystyle\leq\frac{A[i^{\prime}]+B[k^{*}-i^{\prime}]}{2^{\ell}} \displaystyle<\frac{(A*B)[k^{*}]+2^{\ell+1}}{2^{\ell}} \displaystyle<\left\lfloor\frac{(A*B)[k^{*}]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+3. $$

By definition of $P,Q$ and Property 1 of 5.4, it holds that

$$ \left\lfloor\frac{(A*B)[k^{*}]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor-2\leq P[i^{*}]+Q[j^{*}]\leq\left\lfloor\frac{(A*B)[k^{*}]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor. $$

Putting all these bounds together, there must be some $z\in[-4,4]$ such that

$$ R[k^{*}]=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in X\\
i+j=k^{*}\end{subarray}}\left\lfloor\frac{A[i]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{B[j]}{2^{\ell}}\right\rfloor+z=P[i^{*}]+Q[j^{*}], $$

completing the proof of the claim. ∎

In light of 5.5, with high probability over the $100\log n$ trials there is some iteration $\ell,x,y,z$ in which we assign $P[i^{*}]+Q[j^{*}]=R[k^{*}]$ . We argue that in this iteration we correctly assign $C[k^{*}]$ . In step 33.2 we construct the 3SUM instance $(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R})$ , and by definition it contains the solution $(i^{*},P[i^{*}])+(j^{*},Q[j^{*}])=(k^{*},R[k^{*}])$ . Lemma 4.3 guarantees that this solution is either listed in $\mathcal{T}$ , in which case we correctly assign $C[k^{*}]$ in step 33.3, or is part of one of the subinstances $(\mathcal{P}^{\prime},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime},\mathcal{R}^{\prime})$ . In the latter case, focus on the corresponding iteration of step 33.4. By construction, we have $P^{\prime}[i^{*}]=P[i^{*}]$ and $Q^{\prime}[j^{*}]=Q[j^{*}]$ . Thus, $(P^{\prime}*Q^{\prime})[k^{*}]=(P*Q)[k^{*}]$ , recalling that $i^{*}$ is a witness of $(P*Q)[k^{*}]$ by Property 1 of 5.4. Moreover, Property 2 of 5.4 guarantees that every witness $i$ of $(P^{\prime}*Q^{\prime})[k^{*}]$ must be a $2^{\ell}$ -pseudo-witness of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ . However, since $k^{*}$ is relevant at level $\ell$ , there are at most $t$ such pseudo-witnesses, and consequently, $(P^{\prime}*Q^{\prime})[k^{*}]$ has at most $t$ witnesses. We are therefore guaranteed to find $i^{*}$ by the listing algorithm, and thus update $C[k^{*}]$ as intended. This completes the correctness analysis.

Finally, it remains to analyze the running time. Step 1 runs in time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2\rho})$ and step 2 runs in time $\widetilde{O}(n^{1+2\rho})$ . Step 3 runs in $O(\log u)$ iterations. In each iteration, step 33.1 runs in time $O(n+n^{2-2\rho})$ , step 33.2 is dominated by the call to Lemma 4.3 running in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ for some constant $\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ , step 33.3 can be charged to the running time of that lemma as well, and step 33.4 constructs $O(n^{\epsilon})$ Min-Plus Convolution Listing instances, passes them to the reduction, and processes their $O(n^{1+2\rho})$ reported witnesses per instance. The total time is $O((n^{1+2\rho+\epsilon}+n^{2-2\rho}+n^{2-\delta})\log u)$ . This is as claimed, by possibly reducing $\delta$ to account for the second term. ∎

### 5.3 Universe Reduction for Monotone Min-Plus Convolution

Recall that a sequence $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ is monotone if $A[0]\leq A[1]\leq\dots\leq A[n]$ . We refer to the Min-Plus Convolution problem with both input sequences $A,B$ being monotone as the Monotone Min-Plus Convolution problem. We emphasize that this convention applies to Section 5 only; in other parts of this paper (notably, Section 6.3) we often consider the variant where only one of the two input sequences is monotone.

It is easy to see that the general Min-Plus Convolution problem is trivially equivalent to Monotone Min-Plus Convolution: On the one hand, any monotone instance can trivially be regarded as non-monotone. And on the other hand, any non-monotone instance $(A,B)$ over a universe $[u]$ can be converted to the equivalent monotone instance $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime})$ for

$$ \displaystyle A^{\prime}[i] \displaystyle=i\cdot 10u+A[i], \displaystyle B^{\prime}[j] \displaystyle=j\cdot 10u+B[j]. $$

However, this transformation increases the universe size from $u$ to (roughly) $un$ . In this section, we show that a converse transformation exists, from monotone to non-monotone, that reduces the universe size by a factor $n$ . In particular, this shows that Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[u]$ is equivalent to Monotone Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[nu]$ .

#### 5.6Universe Reduction for Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

If Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[u]$ can be solved in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ for some constant $\epsilon>0$ , then Monotone Min-Plus Convolution of the universe $[un]$ can be solved in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}})$ for some constant $\epsilon^{\prime}>0$ . Moreover, the resulting algorithm can provide a witness for each output entry of the Monotone Min-Plus Convolution instance.

A major part of the proof of Lemma 5.6 follows the ideas of Chan and Lewenstein [25]: We impose a coarse-grained grid on the 2-dimensional index set of the given sequences, inducing a partition into cells. For each cell we select some representative point, apply the BSG theorem on these representatives, and may therefore assume that the representatives form a low-doubling set. From then on, our reduction differs, relying on additive hashing rather than sparse convolutions.

Specifically, it is convenient to use on the following covering version of the BSG theorem with an algorithmic proof due to Chan and Lewenstein [25]:

#### 5.7BSG Covering [25].

Let $0<\alpha<1$ , let $t\geq 1$ , let $A,B$ be sets of size at most $n$ , and let $C$ be a set of size at most $tn$ . There are subsets $A_{1},\dots,A_{m}\subseteq A$ and $B_{1},\dots,B_{m}\subseteq B$ and a remainder set $R\subseteq A\times B$ such that:

- (i) $\{(a,b)\in A\times B:a+b\in C\}\subseteq R\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}(A_{i}\times B_{i})$ ,

- (ii) $m=O(\alpha^{-1})$ , and for all $1\leq i\leq m$ , $|A_{i}+B_{i}|\leq O(\alpha^{-5}t^{3}n)$ , and

- (iii) $|R|\leq O(\alpha n^{2})$ .

Moreover, the sets $A_{1},\dots,A_{m},B_{1},\dots,B_{m}$ and $R$ can be computed in time $\widetilde{O}(n^{2})$ by a randomized algorithm.

Let $(A,B)$ denote the given Monotone Min-Plus Convolution instance over the universe $[un]$ (where both $A,B$ are monotone), and rewrite these two sequences as

$$ \displaystyle A[i] \displaystyle=A_{1}[i]\cdot u+A_{0}[i], \displaystyle B[j] \displaystyle=B_{1}[j]\cdot u+B_{0}[j], $$

where $A_{0},B_{0}$ have entries at most $u$ and $A_{1},B_{1}$ have entries at most $n$ . In fact, we may assume without loss of generality that $A_{0}[i],B_{0}[j]<u/2$ (by splitting both sequences into two subsequences, splitting the entries that are less than $u/2$ from the other entries, and computing their four pairwise min-plus convolutions).

Toward computing $A*B$ we maintain a sequence $C$ , initialized with $\bot$ . Over the course of the algorithm we will modify $C$ by updates of the form $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[j]\}$ (so that we never underestimate an output), claiming that, when the algorithm terminates, we have $A*B=C$ . This also means that our algorithm can provide a witness $i$ for each entry $C[k]$ in the final output, as desired.

Let $\delta>0$ be a constant to be determined, let $\Delta_{X}=\lceil n^{\delta}\rceil$ and let $\Delta_{Y}=\lceil n^{2\delta}\rceil$ . Let $X$ denote the multiples of $\Delta_{X}$ in the range $[0,n]$ , and let $Y$ denote the multiples of $\Delta_{Y}$ in the range $[0,n]$ . We will think of $X\times Y$ as a grid in the plane $[0,n]^{2}$ . The multiples of $\Delta_{X}$ (i.e., the vertical axes) are called anchors, and we say that an integer is anchored at the largest anchor smaller than that index. For an anchor $x\in X$ , we define

$$ \displaystyle L_{A}[x] \displaystyle=\min_{x\leq i<x+\Delta_{X}}A[i],\qquad \displaystyle L_{B}[x] \displaystyle=\min_{x\leq j<x+\Delta_{X}}B[j], \displaystyle U_{A}[x] \displaystyle=\max_{x\leq i<x+\Delta_{X}}A[i],\qquad \displaystyle U_{B}[x] \displaystyle=\max_{x\leq j<x+\Delta_{X}}B[j]; $$

i.e., the smallest and largest entries in the respective segments of $A$ and $B$ anchored at $x$ . We call an anchor $x$ $A$ -light if $U_{A}[x]-L_{A}[x]<\Delta_{Y}$ and $A$ -heavy if $U_{A}[x]-L_{A}[x]\geq\Delta_{Y}$ . Similarly define $B$ -light and $B$ -heavy. We say that an index $k$ is heavy if it has a witness, $A[i]+B[j]=(A*B)[k]$ , where $i$ is anchored at an $A$ -heavy anchor or $j$ is anchored at a $B$ -heavy anchor. Otherwise, we call $k$ light. We will now deal with the heavy and light indices $k$ individually.

#### Heavy Anchors

We deal with the heavy indices by brute-force: For all $i\in[0,n]$ anchored at an $A$ -heavy anchor, and all $j\in[0,n]$ , update $C[i+j]\leftarrow\min\{C[i+j],A[i]+B[j]\}$ . Analogously, enumerate all $j\in[0,n]$ anchored at a $B$ -heavy anchor and all $i\in[0,n]$ to perform the same update. This clearly correctly assigns $C[k]$ for all heavy $k$ .

To bound the running time of this step, recall that $A$ and $B$ (and thus also $A_{1}$ and $B_{1}$ ) are monotone. Each $A$ -heavy anchor witnesses a jump from $A[x]$ to $A[x+\Delta_{X}]$ of at least $\Delta_{Y}$ . Thus, there can be at most $O(n/\Delta_{Y})$ $A$ -heavy anchors. But each anchor covers only $\Delta_{X}$ indices, and therefore the running time is $O(n/\Delta_{Y}\cdot\Delta_{X}\cdot n)=O(n^{2-\delta})$ .

#### Light Anchors

To deal with the light indices we rely on the BSG theorem. Let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A} \displaystyle=\{(x,L_{A}[x]):\text{$x\in X$ is $A$-light}\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{B} \displaystyle=\{(y,L_{B}[y]):\text{$y\in X$ is $B$-light}\}. \displaystyle L_{C}[z] \displaystyle=\min\{L_{A}[x]+L_{B}[z-x]:x\in X\text{ is $A$-light and $z-x\in X$ is $B$-light}\}\quad(z\in 2X), \displaystyle\mathcal{C} \displaystyle=\{(z,L_{C}[z]+h):z\in 2X,\,0\leq h<2\Delta_{Y}\}. $$

We apply the BSG Covering Theorem (Theorem 5.7) on $\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}$ with parameters $t=4\Delta_{Y}$ , $\alpha=n^{-\delta}$ and size bound $|X|$ , yielding subsets $\mathcal{A}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{A}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{B}$ and a remainder set $\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B}$ . We enumerate all remainder pairs $((x,L_{A}[x]),(y,L_{B}[y]))\in\mathcal{R}$ . For each such pair, list all indices $i$ anchored at $x$ , and all indices $j$ anchored at $y$ , and update $C[i+j]\leftarrow\min\{C[i+j],A[i]+B[j]\}$ .

Then enumerate all pairs $\mathcal{A}_{\ell},\mathcal{B}_{\ell}$ for $1\leq\ell\leq m$ . Let $X_{\ell}$ be the subset of anchors $x$ appearing in $\mathcal{A}_{\ell}$ , and similarly let $Y_{\ell}$ be the subset of anchors $y$ appearing in $\mathcal{B}_{\ell}$ . Repeat the following steps $100\log n$ times: Let $\hat{p}=\Theta(n\alpha^{-5}t^{3}\Delta_{Y}\log u)$ (for a sufficiently large constant), and let $p$ be a random prime in the range $[\hat{p},2\hat{p}]$ . Then construct the cyclic sequences $P,Q\in([0,u]\cup\{\bot\})^{\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}}$ by

$$ \displaystyle P[\hat{i}] \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{A_{0}[i]}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle{A_{0}[i]}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle{A_{0}[i]}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle{A_{0}[i]}$\hss}}\phantom{B_{0}[j]}&\text{for some arbitrary $i\in[0,n]$ anchored in $X_{\ell}$ with $\hat{i}\equiv i\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i]\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$,}\\
\bot&\text{if such $i$ does not exist,}\end{cases} \displaystyle Q[\hat{j}] \displaystyle=\begin{cases}B_{0}[j]&\text{for some arbitrary $j\in[0,n]$ anchored in $Y_{\ell}$ with $\hat{j}\equiv j\cdot 2n+B_{1}[j]\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$,}\\
\bot&\text{if such $j$ does not exist.}\end{cases} $$

We compute the cyclic min-plus convolution $P*Q$ ; it is well-known that this reduces to $O(1)$ non-cyclic instances. Moreover, we list some witness of $\hat{i}$ for each output entry $(P*Q)[\hat{k}]$ by Lemma 2.14. For each such pair, letting $\hat{j}=\hat{k}-\hat{i}$ , we determine the indices $i$ and $j$ corresponding to $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ that were used in defining $P[\hat{i}]$ and $Q[\hat{j}]$ (via $\hat{i}\equiv i\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i]$ , and analogously for $j$ ) and update $C[i+j]\leftarrow\min\{C[i+j],A[i]+B[j]\}$ .

#### Correctness

Let us analyze the correctness of the light step. Our goal is to show that, for each light index $k$ , we eventually correctly assign $C[k]=(A*B)[k]$ . Fix any such $k$ , let $i$ be a witness of $(A*B)[k]$ , and let $j=k-i$ . Let $x$ be the anchor of $i$ , and let $y$ be the anchor of $j$ . Since $k$ is light, we know that $x$ is $A$ -light and that $y$ is $B$ -light. Thus, $(x,L_{A}[x])\in\mathcal{A}$ and $(y,L_{B}[y])\in\mathcal{B}$ . Let $z=x+y$ . We claim that

$$ L_{A}[x]+L_{B}[y]<L_{C}[z]+2\Delta_{Y}. $$

Suppose otherwise, and let $x^{\prime}+y^{\prime}=z$ be such that $L_{A}[x^{\prime}]+L_{B}[y^{\prime}]=L_{C}[z]$ , $x^{\prime}\in X$ is $A$ -light, and $y^{\prime}\in X$ is $B$ -light. Let $i^{\prime}=i-x+x^{\prime}$ and note that $i^{\prime}$ is anchored at $x^{\prime}$ . Similarly, let $j^{\prime}=j-y+y^{\prime}$ and note that $j^{\prime}$ is anchored at $y^{\prime}$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle A[i^{\prime}]+B[j^{\prime}] \displaystyle\leq U_{A}[x^{\prime}]+U_{B}[y^{\prime}] \displaystyle<L_{A}[x^{\prime}]+L_{B}[y^{\prime}]+2\Delta_{Y} \displaystyle=L_{C}[z]+2\Delta_{Y} \displaystyle\leq L_{A}[x]+L_{B}[y] \displaystyle\leq A[i]+B[j], $$

which, together with $i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}=k$ , contradicts the assumption that $i$ is a witness of $(A*B)[k]$ . Therefore, (8) holds and by definition, $(z,L_{A}[x]+L_{B}[y])\in\mathcal{C}$ .

By Property 1 of Theorem 5.7 there are two possible cases: the pair $((x,L_{A}[x]),(y,L_{B}[y]))$ appears in the remainder $\mathcal{R}$ or in some set $\mathcal{A}_{\ell}\times\mathcal{B}_{\ell}$ . In the former case we directly enumerate the pair $(i,j)$ in the algorithm and set $C[k]$ as intended. So focus on the latter case. Focus on the $\ell$ -th iteration, and let $p$ be a random prime as in the algorithm. Define

$$ \displaystyle\hat{i} \displaystyle=(i\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i])\bmod p, \displaystyle\hat{j} \displaystyle=(j\cdot 2n+B_{1}[j])\bmod p, \displaystyle\hat{k} \displaystyle=(k\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[j])\bmod p. $$

We now argue that three success events happen simultaneously with good probability.

First, $P[\hat{i}]=A_{0}[i]$ , unless there is a collision of the form $i\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i]\equiv i^{\prime}\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i^{\prime}]\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$ . By the Prime Number Theorem, for any fixed $i^{\prime}$ (distinct from $i$ ) this collision takes place only with probability $O(\hat{p}^{-1}\log u)$ . This is at most $1/4n$ by choosing the constant in $\hat{p}$ sufficiently large. Taking a union bound over all $n$ choices of $i^{\prime}$ , it follows that we avoid all collisions with probability at least $3/4$ . Second, we analogously have $Q[\hat{j}]=B_{0}[j]$ with probability at least $3/4$ .

The third success event is that the only indices $i^{\prime},j^{\prime}$ , anchored in $X_{\ell}$ and $Y_{\ell}$ , respectively, and satisfying

$$ (i^{\prime}+j^{\prime})\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i^{\prime}]+B_{1}[j^{\prime}]\equiv\hat{k}\;\,({\bmod}\>p), $$

are those for which $i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}=i+j=k$ and $A_{1}[i^{\prime}]+B_{1}[j^{\prime}]=A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[j]$ . To analyze this event, note that $(i^{\prime}+j^{\prime})\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i^{\prime}]+B_{1}[j^{\prime}]$ takes only $O(|\mathcal{A}_{\ell}+\mathcal{B}_{\ell}|\Delta_{X}\Delta_{Y})$ distinct values. Each undesired value, i.e., each value other than $(i+j)\cdot 2n+A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[j]$ , collides with $\hat{k}$ (modulo $p$ ) with probability at most $O(\hat{p}^{-1}\log u)$ , and thus the error probability is

$$ O\left\lparen\frac{|\mathcal{A}_{\ell}+\mathcal{B}_{\ell}|\Delta_{X}\Delta_{Y}\log u}{\hat{p}}\right\rparen=O\left\lparen\frac{\alpha^{-5}t^{3}|X|\Delta_{X}\Delta_{Y}\log u}{\hat{p}}\right\rparen=O\left\lparen\frac{\alpha^{-5}t^{3}n\Delta_{Y}\log u}{\hat{p}}\right\rparen, $$

by Property 2 of Theorem 5.7. Choosing the constant in $\hat{p}$ sufficiently large, this error probability is at most $1/4$ , say.

All three success events happen simultaneously with probability at least $1/4$ . In this case we have $(P*Q)[\hat{k}]\leq P[\hat{i}]+Q[\hat{j}]=A_{0}[i]+B_{0}[j]$ by the first two events, and

$$ (P*Q)[\hat{k}]\geq\min\{A_{0}[i^{\prime}]+B_{0}[j^{\prime}]:i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}=k,\,A_{1}[i^{\prime}]+B_{1}[j^{\prime}]=A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[j]\} $$

by the third event. Put together, it follows that $(P*Q)[\hat{k}]=A_{0}[i]+B_{0}[j]$ , and that any witness $\hat{i}$ corresponds to a witness $i^{\prime}$ of $k$ . Consequently, we correctly set $C[k]$ . Over the $100\log n$ iterations this event happens at least once with high probability.

#### Running Time

We finally analyze the running time. Suppose that Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[u]$ is in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon>0$ .

The heavy step runs in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ . The light step first applies the BSG Covering theorem (Theorem 5.7) in time $\widetilde{O}(|X|^{2})=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2\delta})$ . We then enumerate all pairs in the remainder $\mathcal{R}$ , and for each such pair further enumerate $\Delta_{X}^{2}$ pairs of indices amounting to time $O(|\mathcal{R}|\Delta_{X}^{2})=O(\alpha|X|^{2}\Delta_{X}^{2})=O(\alpha n^{2})=O(n^{2-\delta})$ , by Property 3 of Theorem 5.7. We then enumerate all $m=O(\alpha^{-1})=O(n^{\delta})$ pairs of sets $\mathcal{A}_{\ell},\mathcal{B}_{\ell}$ , where the upper bound is due to Property 2 of Theorem 5.7, and run $O(\log n)$ repetitions of the randomized construction. In each repetition we construct and solve a length- $\Theta(\hat{p})$ instance of Min-Plus Convolution. Each such instance can be trivially split into $\lceil\hat{p}/n\rceil^{2}$ subinstances of length at most $n$ . The total time to solve these instances is

$$ \widetilde{O}\left\lparen m\cdot\frac{\hat{p}^{2}}{n^{2}}\cdot n^{2-\epsilon}\right\rparen=\widetilde{O}\left\lparen\alpha^{-11}t^{6}\Delta_{Y}^{2}\cdot n^{2-\epsilon}\right\rparen=\widetilde{O}(n^{2+27\delta-\epsilon}). $$

Choosing $\delta=\epsilon/28>0$ , the total running time becomes $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\delta})$ . This is truly subquadratic as claimed. ∎

### 5.4 Large-Universe Reduction

We are finally in the position to complete the large-universe reduction:

#### 5.8Large-Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution.

Assume Hypothesis 1.7. If Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[n]$ can be solved in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ for some constant $\epsilon>0$ , then Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[u]$ can be solved in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}}(\log u)^{O(1)})$ for some constant $\epsilon^{\prime}>0$ .

In other words, Lemma 5.8 states that the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis implies the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis assuming Hypothesis 1.7. This proves Theorem 1.8.

For the proof we will also rely on the following simple covering lemma, which essentially constitutes an instance of the classic greedy algorithm for Set Cover. For a proof see, e.g., [36, Lemma 5.11].

#### 5.9Greedy Covering.

There is a deterministic algorithm that, given sets $X,Y\subseteq[-u,u]$ , computes a set $S\subseteq[-2u,2u]$ of size at most $|Y-X|/|Y|\cdot\ln|X|$ such that $X\subseteq Y+S$ . It runs in time $|Y-X|\,|S|\cdot(\log u)^{O(1)}$ .

Let $\rho,\epsilon>0$ be two constants to be determined. We apply Lemma 5.3 to reduce any given Min-Plus Convolution instance over the universe $[u]$ to $O(n^{\epsilon})$ instances of Min-Plus Convolution Listing with listing threshold $t=O(n^{2\rho})$ . Each such instance $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime})$ is equipped with a $(K=O(n^{\epsilon}),N=O(n^{2-2\rho}))$ -container $H$ for the joint index set $\mathcal{I}(A^{\prime})\cup\mathcal{I}(B^{\prime})$ . Focus on one such instance $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime})$ for now.

Let $\phi:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{Z}$ be the map defined by $\phi(i,a)=i\cdot 10M+a$ , where $M$ is an upper bound on the largest entry in $H$ . Recall that $H\subseteq[2n]\times\mathbb{Z}$ , and that $H$ has doubling at most $K$ . It follows easily that $\phi$ , restricted to $H+H$ , is an isomorphism, and thus $\phi(H)$ also has doubling at most $K$ . Thus, we may apply Hypothesis 1.7 on the integer set $\phi(H)$ . This yields a subset $Y\subseteq\phi(H)$ of size at least

$$ |Y|\geq\Omega\left\lparen\frac{|H|}{K^{c}}\right\rparen, $$

and a sum-order-preserving hash function $h:Y\to\{0,\dots,N\}$ , where $c$ is the constant from Hypothesis 1.7. Next, apply Lemma 5.9 to compute a set of shifts $S$ such that $\phi(H)\subseteq Y+S$ and such that

$$ |S|\leq\frac{|Y-\phi(H)|}{|Y|}\cdot\ln|H|=O\left\lparen K^{c}\cdot\frac{|\phi(H)-\phi(H)|}{|H|}\cdot\log|H|\right\rparen=O\lparen K^{c+2}\log|H|\rparen, $$

where the last step is due to the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality (Lemma 2.1).

Next, we apply Lemma 2.14 to reduce the Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime})$ with listing threshold $t=O(n^{2\rho})$ to $\widetilde{O}(n^{2\rho})$ plain Min-Plus Convolution subinstances (i.e., for which we do not have to list multiple witnesses). In what follows, fix any such instance, denoted $(A,B)$ ; we argue that it reduces to few instances of Monotone Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[n^{2}]$ . By Lemma 5.6, any such instance further reduces to (non-Monotone) Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[n]$ . Let $C$ be the output sequence, initialized to $\bot$ . We will only update $C$ by updates of the form $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[k-i]\}$ , guaranteeing that no output is underestimated.

Enumerate all shifts $s,t\in S$ . For each pair, construct the sequences $A_{s},B_{t}\in([0,N]\cup\{\bot\})^{[0,n]}$ defined by

$$ \displaystyle A_{s}[i] \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle{h(\phi(i,A[i])-s)}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle{h(\phi(i,A[i])-s)}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle{h(\phi(i,A[i])-s)}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle{h(\phi(i,A[i])-s)}$\hss}}\phantom{h(\phi(j,B[j])-t)}&\text{if $\phi(i,A[i])\in Y+s$,}\\
\bot&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} \displaystyle B_{t}[j] \displaystyle=\begin{cases}h(\phi(j,B[j])-t)&\text{if $\phi(j,B[j])\in Y+t$,}\\
\bot&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Note that both sequences are almost monotone: The sequence $\phi(i,A[i])$ is increasing for $i=0,\dots,n$ (when restricted to the non- $\bot$ entries), and hence, so are the images of $\phi(i,A[i])-s\in Y$ under the order-preserving function $h$ . To remove the $\bot$ entries simply replace both sequences by their suffix-minima, i.e., replace $A_{s}$ and $B_{t}$ by

$$ \displaystyle A_{s}^{\prime}[i] \displaystyle=\min_{i^{\prime}\geq i}A_{s}[i^{\prime}], \displaystyle B_{t}^{\prime}[j] \displaystyle=\min_{j^{\prime}\geq j}B_{t}[j^{\prime}]. $$

We compute the Monotone Min-Plus Convolution $A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime}$ using the reduction provided by Lemma 5.6. Moreover, by Lemma 5.6, we know one witness $i$ per output $(A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k]$ ; then update $C[k]\leftarrow\min\{C[k],A[i]+B[k-i]\}$ .

#### Correctness

We argue that once the algorithm stops, we have correctly assigned $C$ . Fix any witness $i^{*}$ of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ , and let $j^{*}=k^{*}-i^{*}$ . Since $H$ is a container of the index sets $\mathcal{I}(A)$ and $\mathcal{I}(B)$ , we must have $(i^{*},A[i^{*}]),(j^{*},B[j^{*}])\in H$ . Thus, by $\phi(H)\subseteq Y+S$ , there exist $s,t\in S$ such that $\phi(i^{*},A[i^{*}])\in Y+s$ and $\phi(j^{*},B[j^{*}])\in Y+t$ . Focus on the iteration associated with that pair $s,t$ .

We first claim that any witness $i$ of $(A_{s}*B_{t})[k^{*}]$ must also be a witness of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ . Indeed, take any other pair $i+j=k^{*}$ and assume that $i$ is not a witness of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ , i.e.,

$$ A[i^{*}]+B[j^{*}]<A[i]+B[j]. $$

Then clearly also

$$ \phi(i^{*},A[i^{*}])+\phi(j^{*},B[j^{*}])<\phi(i,A[i])+\phi(j,B[j]), $$

and thus,

$$ (\phi(i^{*},A[i^{*}])-s)+(\phi(j^{*},B[j^{*}])-t)<(\phi(i,A[i])-s)+(\phi(j,B[j])-t), $$

But $h$ is sum-order-preserving and therefore,

$$ A_{s}[i^{*}]+B_{t}[j^{*}]<A_{s}[i]+B_{t}[j], $$

for all non- $\bot$ entries, so $i$ cannot be a witness of $(A_{s}*B_{t})[k^{*}]$ . This proves that any witness $i$ of $(A_{s}*B_{t})[k^{*}]$ is also a witness of $(A*B)[k^{*}]$ (though the converse is not necessarily true; notably, $i^{*}$ is not necessarily a witness of $(A_{s}*B_{t})[k^{*}]$ ).

We finally argue that any witness of $(A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]$ is also a witness of $(A_{s}*B_{t})[k^{*}]$ . Let $i$ be a witness of $(A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]$ . Let $j=k^{*}-i.$ By definition, there exist $i^{\prime}\geq i$ and $j^{\prime}\geq j$ such that

$$ (A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]=A_{s}[i^{\prime}]+B_{t}[j^{\prime}]. $$

Suppose that $i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}>k^{*}$ . Then

$$ \phi(i^{*},A[i^{*}])+\phi(j^{*},B[j^{*}])<\phi(i^{\prime},A[i^{\prime}])+\phi(j^{\prime},B[j^{\prime}]), $$

and thus by the same reasoning as above,

$$ A_{s}[i^{*}]+B_{t}[j^{*}]<A_{s}[i^{\prime}]+B_{t}[j^{\prime}]. $$

But then we reach the contradiction that

$$ (A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]\leq A^{\prime}_{s}[i^{*}]+B^{\prime}_{t}[j^{*}]\leq A_{s}[i^{*}]+B_{t}[j^{*}]<A_{s}[i^{\prime}]+B_{t}[j^{\prime}]=(A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}], $$

and must have $i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}=k^{*}$ instead. Combined with $i^{\prime}\geq i$ , $j^{\prime}\geq j$ and $i+j=k^{*}$ , we conclude that $i=i^{\prime}$ and $j=j^{\prime}$ . Recall that we initially picked $i$ as an arbitrary witness of $(A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]$ . We have thus argued that

$$ (A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]=\min_{i+j=k^{*}}(A_{s}[i]+B_{t}[j]), $$

and so the witnesses of $(A_{s}^{\prime}*B_{t}^{\prime})[k^{*}]$ and $(A_{s}*B_{t})[k^{*}]$ are identical.

#### Running Time

Initially, we call Lemma 5.3 to reduce from one given instance to $O(n^{\epsilon})$ listing instances, each provided with a low-doubling container. Lemma 5.3 runs in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ for some constant $\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0$ . For each instance we call the algorithm implied by Hypothesis 1.7 on the container set $\phi(H)$ . This set has size $N=O(n^{2-2\rho})$ and doubling $K=O(n^{\epsilon})$ , and so this takes time $O(n^{2-2\rho+O(\epsilon)})$ . We then apply Lemma 5.9 in time

$$ |Y-\phi(H)|\,|S|(\log u)^{O(1)}=NK^{2c+2}(\log u)^{O(1)}=n^{2-2\rho+O(\epsilon)}(\log u)^{O(1)}. $$

Then we reduce each listing instance (with threshold $t=O(n^{2\rho})$ ) further to $\widetilde{O}(n^{2\rho})$ plain Min-Plus Convolution subinstances by Lemma 2.14. This leaves us with $\widetilde{O}(n^{2\rho+\epsilon})$ instances that the main part of the algorithm treats. For each pair of shifts $s,t\in S$ we construct the sequences $A_{s},B_{t}$ and $A_{s}^{\prime},B_{t}^{\prime}$ in linear time. Assuming the premise of Lemma 5.8, by Lemma 5.6 we can compute their convolution in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon_{0}})$ for some $\epsilon_{0}>0$ . The total time is

$$ \left\lparen n^{2-\delta}+n^{2-2\rho+O(\epsilon)}+n^{2\rho+\epsilon+2-\epsilon_{0}}\right\rparen(\log u)^{O(1)}. $$

This becomes subquadratic for, say, $\rho=\epsilon_{0}/8$ and by choosing $0<\epsilon\leq\epsilon_{0}/2$ sufficiently small so that the $O(\epsilon)$ term becomes at most $\rho$ . ∎

## 6 Lower Bounds for Intermediate Convolution Problems

In this section, we show our lower bounds for intermediate problems under the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis (also under the standard Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis if we assume Hypothesis 1.7).

We start with a useful lemma, which separately handles those heavy input entries.

#### 6.1.

Let $(A,B)$ be a given Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance with listing threshold $n^{\ell}$ for some $\ell\geq 1/2$ . Suppose $C=A*B$ is also given and let $\delta>0$ be a given constant. Then in $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\delta/2})$ time, we can reduce it to a Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance $(A,B^{\prime})$ , where all entries in $B$ that appear more than $n^{\ell+\delta}$ times are replaced with $\perp$ .

Call a value $v$ in $B$ heavy if it appears more than $n^{\ell+\delta}$ times in $B$ . Note that there could be at most $O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})$ heavy value $v$ . It suffices to list up to $n^{\ell}$ witnesses $(i,j)$ per output $C[k]$ , among those witnesses where $B[j]$ is a heavy element.

To do so, let $v$ be an arbitrary heavy element in $B$ , and define $J_{v}=\{j\in[0,n]:B[j]=v\}$ . For every distinct value $u$ in $A$ , define $I_{u}=\{i\in[0,n]:A[i]=u\}$ and $K_{u+v}=\{k\in[0,2n]:C[k]=u+v\}$ . These sets can be precomputed in near-linear time. Clearly, a pair $(i,j)\in I_{u}\times J_{v}$ is a witness for $C[i+j]$ if $i+j\in K_{u+v}$ .

For a fixed pair of $u,v$ , using FFT, we can verify whether each $k\in K_{u+v}$ has a witness from $I_{u}\times J_{v}$ in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ total time for all $k$ . Moreover, using standard sampling-based approaches (Lemma 2.15), we can list up to $\lfloor\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor$ witnesses per $k\in K_{u+v}$ in $\widetilde{O}(\lfloor\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor n+1)$ time. The $+1$ term in the previous running time is needed for the case $\lfloor\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor=0$ . Over all values of $v$ and $u$ , the total cost for this case is thus (up to $\polylog(n)$ factor)

$$ \sum_{u}\sum_{v}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\right\rfloor n+1\right)\leq n^{1-\ell-\delta}\sum_{u}\left(\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\cdot n+1\right)\leq O(n^{2-\delta/2}). $$

Hence, it suffices to consider some $k\in K_{u+v}$ for sub-instances $(I_{u},J_{v},K_{u+v})$ where $k$ has at least $\lfloor\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor$ witnesses (and we have not found up to $n^{\ell}$ witnesses in the input instance $(A,B)$ for $k$ ). In this case, we simply spend $O(|I_{u}|)$ time to list all the witnesses for $k$ in $(I_{u},J_{v},K_{u+v})$ . Let $U_{k}$ be the set of $u$ where we need to perform this brute-force over $I_{u}$ for $k$ . Note that for a fixed $k$ , $C[k]=u+v$ is fixed; in addition, the number of heavy values $v$ is $O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})$ , so the number of $u$ where $k\in K_{u+v}$ is also $O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})$ . Hence $|U_{k}|\leq O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})$ .

As we only need to output $n^{\ell}$ total witnesses for $k$ , we have

$$ \sum_{u\in U_{k}}\left\lfloor\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\right\rfloor\leq n^{\ell}, $$

which implies (recall we assume $\ell\geq 1/2$ )

$$ \sum_{u\in U_{k}}\frac{|I_{u}|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\leq|U_{k}|+n^{\ell}\leq n^{1-\ell-\delta}+n^{\ell}=O(n^{\ell}). $$

Hence, the cost for a particular value of $k$ is

$$ O\left(\sum_{u\in U_{k}}|I_{u}|\right)\leq O(n^{\ell}\cdot n^{1-\ell-\delta/2})=O(n^{1-\delta/2}). $$

Summing over all possible $k$ gives an $O(n^{2-\delta/2})$ running time, as desired. ∎

### 6.1 Min-Max Convolution

See 1.9
