Suppose Min-Max Convolution can be solved in $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ time for some $\epsilon>0$ by an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ . In order to show this contradicts the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, by Corollary 5.2 with $\gamma=\frac{1}{2}$ , it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution instances $(A,B)$ where the elements are from $[\sqrt{n}]$ while we need to list up to $\sqrt{n}$ witnesses per output.

Because the universe is $[\sqrt{n}]$ , $C=A*B$ can be computed in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ time. By Lemma 6.1, we can further assume every non- $\perp$ value in $B$ appears at most $n^{1/2+\epsilon/3}$ times.

For every $b\in[\sqrt{n}]$ , we define a Min-Max Convolution instance $(A_{b},B_{b})$ , where $A_{b}[i]=A[i]$ for every $i\in[0,n]$ , and $B_{b}[j]=-\infty$ if $B[j]=b$ and $B_{b}[j]=\infty$ otherwise. Let $C_{b}=\MinMax(A_{b},B_{b})$ . It is not difficult to see that, $(i,j)$ is a witness for $C[k]$ (i.e., $A[i]+B[j]=C[k]$ and $i+j=k$ ), if and only if for some $b$ , $C_{b}[k]=C[k]-b$ and $(i,j)$ is a witness for $C_{b}[k]$ in the Min-Max Convolution instance defined for $b$ .

Consider the following algorithm. We enumerate $b\in[\sqrt{n}]$ , create $A_{b}$ and $B_{b}$ , and compute $C_{b}=\MinMax(A_{b},B_{b})$ using $\mathcal{A}$ in $O(n^{1.5-\epsilon})$ time per $b$ . By standard sampling-based approaches (Lemma 2.14), we can further list $n^{2\epsilon/3}$ witnesses for every $C_{b}[k]$ in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5-\epsilon/3})$ time using $\mathcal{A}$ as a black-box. This step takes $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\cdot n^{1.5-\epsilon/3})=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\epsilon/3})$ time over all $b\in[\sqrt{n}]$ .

What remains to consider are those $C_{b}[k]$ that have more than $n^{2\epsilon/3}$ witnesses and $C_{b}[k]=C[k]-b$ . We call such a pair $(b,k)$ heavy. For a heavy pair, we enumerate all elements in $S_{b}:=\{j\in[n]:B[j]=b\}$ (this can be done in $O(|S_{b}|)$ time by computing these sets in preprocessing), and check whether each $j\in S_{b}$ forms a witness for $C_{b}[k]$ . Recall each value in $B$ appears at most $n^{1/2+\epsilon/3}$ time, so the cost for each heavy pair is $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3})$ . Since we only need to list up to $n^{1/2}$ witness per $C[k]$ , we only need to resolve $n^{1/2-2\epsilon/3}$ heavy pairs for a particular value of $k$ before we find enough witnesses for $C[k]$ . Hence, we only need to handle $O(n^{3/2-2\epsilon/3})$ heavy pairs in total, and thus the overall running time for this case is $O(n^{2-\epsilon/3})$ . ∎

### 6.2 Min-Equality Convolution

See 1.10

Suppose Min-Equality Convolution can be solved in $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ time for some $\epsilon>0$ by an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ . Similar as before, it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution Listing instances $(A,B)$ where the elements are from $[\sqrt{n}]$ while we need to list up to $\sqrt{n}$ witnesses per output.

We can compute $C=A*B$ in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ time and we can further assume every non- $\perp$ value in $B$ appears at most $n^{1/2+\epsilon/3}$ time by Lemma 6.1.

For every $\Delta\in\{-\sqrt{n},\ldots,\sqrt{n}\}$ , we define a Min-Equality Convolution instance $(A_{\Delta},B_{\Delta})$ , where $A_{\Delta}[i]=A[i]+\Delta$ for every $i\in[0,n]$ and $B_{\Delta}=B$ . Intuitively, we aim to use $\Delta$ to represent $B[j]-A[i]$ . Let $C_{\Delta}=\MinEqual(A_{\Delta},B_{\Delta})$ . The following claim shows how the witnesses in the Min-Equality Convolution instance $(A_{\Delta},B_{\Delta})$ are related to the witnesses in the Min-Plus Convolution instance $(A,B)$ .

#### 6.2.

Let $(i_{0},j_{0},k_{0})\in[0,n]^{3}$ be a triple with $i_{0}+j_{0}=k_{0}$ , and let $\Delta=B[j_{0}]-A[i_{0}]$ . Then, $A[i_{0}]+B[j_{0}]=C[k_{0}]$ holds if and only if both $2C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]=C[k_{0}]+\Delta$ and $A_{\Delta}[i_{0}]=B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]=C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]$ hold.

We first show the forward direction. By definition,

$$ \displaystyle 2C_{\Delta}[k_{0}] \displaystyle=2\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j=k_{0}\\
A_{\Delta}[i]=B_{\Delta}[j]\end{subarray}}B_{\Delta}[j]=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j=k_{0}\\
A[i]+\Delta=B[j]\end{subarray}}\{A[i]+\Delta+B[j]\} \displaystyle\geq\min_{i+j=k_{0}}\{A[i]+\Delta+B[j]\}=C[k_{0}]+\Delta. $$

Additionally, since $A_{\Delta}[i_{0}]=A[i_{0}]+\Delta=B[j_{0}]=B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]$ ,

$$ 2C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]\leq 2B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]=A[i_{0}]+\Delta+B[j_{0}]=C[k_{0}]+\Delta. $$

Hence, we have $2C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]=C[k_{0}]+\Delta$ . Moreover, we have $C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]=B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]$ since the above inequality is tight, so $A_{\Delta}[i_{0}]=B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]=C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]$ holds as claimed.

Now we consider the reverse direction. From the assumptions $2C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]=C[k_{0}]+\Delta$ and $A_{\Delta}[i_{0}]=B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]=C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]$ , we have

$$ C[k_{0}]+\Delta=2C_{\Delta}[k_{0}]=A_{\Delta}[i_{0}]+B_{\Delta}[j_{0}]=A[i_{0}]+\Delta+B[j_{0}], $$

so $A[i_{0}]+B[j_{0}]=C[k_{0}]$ holds as claimed. ∎

Consider the following algorithm. We enumerate $\Delta\in\{-\sqrt{n},\ldots,\sqrt{n}\}$ , create $A_{\Delta}$ and $B_{\Delta}$ , and compute $C_{\Delta}=\MinEqual(A_{\Delta},B_{\Delta})$ using $\mathcal{A}$ in $O(n^{1.5-\epsilon})$ time per $\Delta$ . By standard sampling-based approaches (Lemma 2.14), we can further list $n^{2\epsilon/3}$ witnesses for every $C_{\Delta}$ in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5-\epsilon/3})$ time using $\mathcal{A}$ as a black-box. This step takes $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\cdot n^{1.5-\epsilon/3})=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\epsilon/3})$ over all $\Delta$ .

What remains to consider are those $C_{\Delta}[k]$ that have more than $n^{2\epsilon/3}$ witnesses and $2C_{\Delta}[k]=C[k]+\Delta$ . We call such a pair $(\Delta,k)$ heavy. By 6.2, the set of witnesses for $C_{\Delta}[k]$ is exactly the set of $(i,j)$ where $A[i]+B[j]=C[k]$ and $B[j]-A[i]=\Delta$ . Since the values of $C[k]$ and $\Delta$ are both known, we can determine the value $A[i]=u$ and $B[j]=v$ where $u=(C[k]-\Delta)/2,v=(C[k]+\Delta)/2$ . After simple linear time preprocessing, we can enumerate elements in the set $S_{v}=\{j\in[n]:B[j]=v\}$ in $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3})$ time (recall each element can appear at most $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3})$ times in $B$ ). Once we have this set, we can compute the exact set of witnesses for $C_{\Delta}[k]$ in $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3})$ time, simply by checking if $A_{\Delta}[k-j]=B_{\Delta}[j]$ and compare them with $C_{\Delta}[k]$ for $j\in S_{v}$ . Since we only need to list up to $n^{1/2}$ witness per $C[k]$ , we only need to resolve $n^{1/2-2\epsilon/3}$ heavy pairs for a particular value of $k$ before we find enough witnesses for $C[k]$ . Hence, we only need to handle $O(n^{3/2-2\epsilon/3})$ heavy pairs, and thus the overall running time for this case is $O(n^{2-\epsilon/3})$ . ∎

### 6.3 Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution

In order to show the hardness for Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution, we first show the hardness of another problem in the following:

#### 6.3.

Let $A\in[\sqrt{n}]^{[0,n]}$ and $B\in[\sqrt{n}]^{[0,{\sqrt{n}}]}$ . Computing the Min-Plus Convolution between $A$ and $B$ requires $n^{1.5-o(1)}$ time, under the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be such an $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ time algorithm. Similar as before, it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution instances $(A,B)$ where the elements are from $[\sqrt{n}]$ while we need to list up to $\sqrt{n}$ witnesses per output.

By trying all sampling rates $p=1,2^{-1},2^{-2},\ldots$ , and only keeping sampled elements in $B$ as their original values while setting all other elements as $\perp$ , then with high probability, there will be a round where the number of witnesses for $C[k]$ is $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ if the number of witnesses for $C[k]$ in the original instance is more than $\sqrt{n}$ . Hence, we only need to handle $C[k]$ with $O(\sqrt{n})$ witnesses. By padding the sequences with $O(n)$ additional $\perp$ ’s, we can further assume that we only need to handle $C[k]$ with $\sqrt{n}$ witnesses.

Let $N$ be a prime number from $[2n,4n]$ , which can be found deterministically in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ time. We extend $A$ and $B$ to length $N$ , where the extra elements are padded as $\perp$ . Now the Min-Plus Convolution $C$ between $A$ and $B$ can be equivalently defined by $C[k]=\min_{i\in\mathbb{F}_{N}}\{A[i]+B[k-i]\}$ .

We repeat the following $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ iterations: sample $x\sim\mathbb{F}_{N}\setminus\{0\}$ and $y\sim\mathbb{F}_{N}$ . Create a length- $N$ sequence $A^{\prime}$ where $A^{\prime}[xi]=A[i]$ for every $i\in\mathbb{F}_{N}$ ; create a length- $\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor$ sequence $B^{\prime}$ where $B^{\prime}[xj+y]=B[j]$ if $xj+y\in\{0,1,\ldots,\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\}$ . We can use $\mathcal{A}$ to compute $C^{\prime}=A^{\prime}*B^{\prime}$ in $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ time. By the standard sampling-based approach (Lemma 2.14 generalized to input sequences of different lengths), we can also list a witness for each $C^{\prime}[k]$ in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ time, by using $\mathcal{A}$ as a black-box. Observe that, if some $C[k]$ has witnesses $(i,j)$ where $A[i]+B[j]=C[k]$ , and if $xj+y\in\{0,1,\ldots,\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\}$ , then $(xi,xj+y)$ will be a witness for $C^{\prime}[xk+y]$ . Given a witness for $C^{\prime}[xk+y]$ , we can convert it back to a witness for $C[k]$ . By repeating $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ iterations, we can list multiple witnesses for $C[k]$ , though there might be repeated witnesses from different iterations. It remains to analyze the success probability of collecting all witnesses for each $C[k]$ .

Let $J_{k}$ be the set of $j\in\mathbb{F}_{N}$ where $j$ is a witness for $C[k]$ (i.e., $A[k-j]+B[j]=C[k]$ ). Recall we only need to list witnesses for $C[k]$ where $|J_{k}|\leq\sqrt{n}$ . Let $j_{0}\in J_{k}$ be an arbitrary witness, and we focus on a particular iteration. Let $X_{j}$ denote the event that $B[j]=B^{\prime}[xj+y]$ in this iteration, i.e., $xj+y\in\{0,1,\ldots,\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\}$ . If only $X_{j_{0}}$ happens, and $X_{j}$ does not happen for other $j\in J_{k}\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ , then the algorithm is able to discover $j_{0}$ as a witness for $C[k]$ in this iteration. Using the near-independence between $X_{j^{\prime}}$ and $X_{j}$ for $j\neq j^{\prime}$ by the way we sample $x$ and $y$ , this happens with probability

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left[X_{j_{0}}\wedge\bigwedge_{j\in J_{k}\setminus\{j_{0}\}}\neg X_{j}\right] \displaystyle=\Pr\left[X_{j_{0}}\right]-\Pr\left[X_{j_{0}}\wedge\bigvee_{j\in J_{k}\setminus\{j_{0}\}}X_{j}\right] \displaystyle\geq\Pr\left[X_{j_{0}}\right]-\sum_{j\in J_{k}\setminus\{j_{0}\}}\Pr\left[X_{j_{0}}\wedge X_{j}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor+1}{N}-(|J_{k}|-1)\cdot\frac{\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor+1}{N}\cdot\frac{\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor}{N-1} \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}-\sqrt{n}\cdot\left(\frac{\sqrt{N}+1}{N}\right)^{2} \displaystyle=\Omega(N^{-1/2}), $$

where the last step is because $n\leq N/2$ . Hence, in $\widetilde{O}(N^{1/2})$ iterations, we can list all witnesses for $C[k]$ with high probability. ∎

See 1.11

By Lemma 6.3, it suffices to reduce the problem of computing the Min-Plus Convolution between $A\in[\sqrt{n}]^{[0,n]}$ and $B\in[\sqrt{n}]^{[0,\sqrt{n}]}$ to bounded-monotone Min-Plus Convolution. By padding, we can assume $\sqrt{n}$ is an integer for convenience.

We first carefully split $A$ to two halves $A^{\text{odd}}$ and $A^{\text{even}}$ , where

$$ A^{\text{odd}}[i]=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lr}A[i]&\text{if $\lfloor i/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is odd,}\\
\infty&\text{if $\lfloor i/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is even,}\end{array}\right.\quad\quad A^{\text{even}}[i]=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lr}\infty&\text{if $\lfloor i/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is odd,}\\
A[i]&\text{if $\lfloor i/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is even.}\end{array}\right. $$

It suffices to separately compute $A^{\text{odd}}*B$ and $A^{\text{even}}*B$ , and combine the results. As the methods are essentially the same for these two Min-Plus Convolutions, we focus on computing $C^{\text{odd}}=A^{\text{odd}}*B$ .

Create sequences $A^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ and $B^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ , where

$$ A^{\prime}[i]=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lr}A[i]+\sqrt{n}\cdot(i\bmod\sqrt{n})&\text{if $\lfloor i/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is odd,}\\
10n&\text{if $\lfloor i/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is even,}\end{array}\right.\quad\quad B^{\prime}[j]=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lr}B[j]+\sqrt{n}\cdot j&\text{if $j\leq\sqrt{n}$,}\\
10n&\text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right. $$

By definition, all entries of $A^{\prime},B^{\prime}$ are non-negative integers in $O(n)$ . Moreover, observe that $B^{\prime}$ is monotone. Hence, we can use a bounded-monotone Min-Plus Convolution algorithm to compute $C^{\prime}=A^{\prime}*B^{\prime}$ . First, observe that $C^{\text{odd}}[k]=\infty$ if and only if $C^{\prime}[k]\geq 10n$ . Now consider the case where $C^{\prime}[k]<10n$ . In this case,

$$ \displaystyle C^{\prime}[k] \displaystyle=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\min\{k,\sqrt{n}\}\\
\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}\left\{A^{\prime}[k-j]+B^{\prime}[j]\right\} \displaystyle=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\min\{k,\sqrt{n}\}\\
\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}\left\{A[k-j]+B[j]+((k-j)\bmod\sqrt{n}+j)\cdot\sqrt{n}\right\} $$

We can simplify the term $(k-j)\bmod\sqrt{n}+j$ via

$$ (k-j)\bmod\sqrt{n}+j=k-j-\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\cdot\sqrt{n}+j=k-\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\cdot\sqrt{n}. $$

Because $0\leq j\leq\sqrt{n}$ , $\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\in[\lfloor(k-\sqrt{n})/\sqrt{n}\rfloor,\lfloor k/\sqrt{n}\rfloor]$ . Notice that there are exactly two integer values in this range. Combined with the condition that $\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is odd, there can actually be only one valid value, which can be computed in $O(1)$ time. Once $\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor$ is determined, we can compute $k-\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\cdot\sqrt{n}$ , and we denote this value by $f_{\text{odd}}(k)$ . Hence, we can further simplify the expression for $C^{\prime}[k]$ as

$$ \displaystyle C^{\prime}[k] \displaystyle=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\min\{k,\sqrt{n}\}\\
\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}\left\{A[k-j]+B[j]+f_{\text{odd}}(k)\cdot\sqrt{n}\right\} \displaystyle=\left(f_{\text{odd}}(k)\cdot\sqrt{n}\right)+\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\min\{k,\sqrt{n}\}\\
\lfloor(k-j)/\sqrt{n}\rfloor\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}\left\{A[k-j]+B[j]\right\} \displaystyle=\left(f_{\text{odd}}(k)\cdot\sqrt{n}\right)+C^{\text{odd}}[k]. $$

Hence, we can compute $C^{\text{odd}}$ from $C^{\prime}$ in linear time, which completes the proof. ∎

### 6.4 Min-Witness Convolution

The following lemma is the key step in the reduction to Min-Witness Convolution.

#### 6.4.

Suppose Min-Witness Convolution can be solved in $O(T(n))$ time, and let $1/3\leq\ell\leq 1$ be a constant. Then in $\widetilde{O}(T(n)\cdot n^{\ell})$ time we can list up to $n^{\ell}$ witnesses for each output in Min-Plus Convolution instances $(A,B)$ where the universe of all elements in $A$ has size $n^{1/3}$ , and the universe of all elements in $B$ is $\{0,\perp\}$ . The algorithm succeeds with high probability.

First, since $B[j]\in\{0,\perp\}$ , we can replace each element in $A$ by its rank in the universe without loss of generality, and hence assume that the universe of elements in $A$ is $[n^{1/3}]$ . Let $C=A*B$ , which can be computed in $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ time.

By trying all sampling rates $p=1,2^{-1},2^{-2},\ldots$ , and only keeping sampled elements in $B$ as their original values while setting all other elements as $\perp$ , then with high probability, there will be a round where the number of witnesses for $C[k]$ is $\Theta(n^{\ell})$ if the number of witnesses for $C[k]$ in the original instance is more than $n^{\ell}$ . Hence, we only need to handle $C[k]$ with $O(n^{\ell})$ witnesses.

In addition, it suffices to list $n^{1/3}$ witnesses per $C[k]$ in $\widetilde{O}(T(n)n^{1/3})$ time: If $\ell>1/3$ , we can randomly partition $B$ to $\Theta(n^{\ell-1/3})$ random subsequences (by keeping elements not in the corresponding subsequence as $\perp$ ), so that for every $C[k]$ , each subsequence contains at most $n^{1/3}$ witnesses, with high probability.

Before we give the actual reduction, let us first give some intuition. The difficulty of reducing Min-Plus Convolution to Min-Witness Convolution is that, in Min-Witness Convolution, there is no value in the inputs. Hence, we somehow need to encode the weight information in the indices. One potential way is to take monotone subsequences of $A$ , and create Boolean sequence $A^{\prime}$ where $A^{\prime}[i]=1$ if $i$ is in the chosen subsequence and create Boolean sequence $B^{\prime}$ where $B^{\prime}[i]=1$ if $B[i]=0$ . Because the chosen subsequence is monotone, the Min-Witness Convolution naturally favors candidates $(i,k-i)$ where $A[i]$ is smaller, as intended. One potential way to choose monotone subsequences is the following: We take all the $1$ ’s in the first $n^{2/3}$ entries of $A$ , all the $2$ ’s in the second $n^{2/3}$ entries of $A$ , and so on. The downside is that, some $C[k]$ might have many witnesses from the subsequence, while some have few. To overcome this issue, we randomly shuffle the indices and work over the shuffled sequences.

Let $N$ be a prime number from $[2n,4n]$ , which can be found deterministically in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ time. We extend $A$ and $B$ to length $N$ , where the extra elements are $\perp$ . Now Min-Plus Convolution $C$ between $A$ and $B$ can be equivalently defined by $C[k]=\min_{i\in\mathbb{F}_{N}}\{A[i]+B[k-i]\}$ .

We will repeat the following $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3})$ times. Let $x\sim\mathbb{F}_{N}\setminus\{0\}$ and $y\sim\mathbb{F}_{N}$ be uniformly random, and let $f_{x,y}:\mathbb{F}_{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{N}$ where $f_{x,y}(i)=i\cdot x+y$ . Now define the shuffled sequences $A_{x,y}$ and $B_{x,y}$ , where

$$ A_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]=A[i]\quad\text{and}\quad B_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]=B[i]\quad\text{for }i\in\mathbb{F}_{N}. $$

$A_{x,y}$ and $B_{x,y}$ are well-defined because $f_{x,y}$ is invertible. Consider two subsets $S_{x,y}=\{i\in\mathbb{F}_{N}:A_{x,y}[i]=\lfloor i/N^{2/3}\rfloor\}$ and $T_{x,y}=\{i\in\mathbb{F}_{N}:B_{x,y}[i]=0\}$ . We then create two Boolean sequences $A^{\prime}_{x,y}$ and $B^{\prime}_{x,y}$ , which are the indicator sequences for $S_{x,y}$ and $T_{x,y}$ respectively.

The following claim shows why it is useful to compute the Min-Witness Convolution between $A^{\prime}_{x,y}$ and $B^{\prime}_{x,y}$ (even though the indices of them are from $\mathbb{F}_{N}$ rather than $\mathbb{Z}$ , we can still use standard Min-Witness Convolution with some simple postprocessing to compute it).

#### 6.5.

Let $I_{k}$ be the set of witnesses for $C[k]$ in the Min-Plus convolution $C=A*B$ . If there is exactly one witness $i\in I_{k}$ such that $f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}$ , then $\MinWitness(A^{\prime}_{x,y},B^{\prime}_{x,y})[x\cdot k+2y]=f_{x,y}(i)$ .

Let $j=k-i$ . Since $i$ is a witness for $C[k]$ , we must have $B[j]\neq\bot$ and hence $B[j]=0$ , and $A[i]=C[k]$ . By definition, clearly $A^{\prime}_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]=1$ , and $B^{\prime}_{x,y}[(x\cdot k+2y)-f_{x,y}(i)]=B^{\prime}_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(j)]=1$ . Hence, $f_{x,y}(i)$ is a witness in the Boolean convolution between $A^{\prime}_{x,y}$ and $B^{\prime}_{x,y}$ . It remains to show that it is the minimum such index.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there exists $t<f_{x,y}(i)$ where $A^{\prime}_{x,y}[t]=B^{\prime}_{x,y}[(x\cdot k+2y)-t]=1$ . By definition, these imply

$$ A_{x,y}[t]=\lfloor t/N^{2/3}\rfloor\quad\text{and}\quad B_{x,y}[(x\cdot k+2y)-t]=0. $$

Because $f_{x,y}$ is invertible, there exists $i^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{N}$ such that $f_{x,y}(i^{\prime})=t$ , and correspondingly $f_{x,y}(k-i^{\prime})=(x\cdot k+2y)-t$ . Hence, we further obtain

$$ A[i^{\prime}]=\lfloor t/N^{2/3}\rfloor\quad\text{and}\quad B[k-i^{\prime}]=0. $$

By the fact $f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}$ , we have $A_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]=\lfloor f_{x,y}(i)/N^{2/3}\rfloor\geq\lfloor t/N^{2/3}\rfloor=A[i^{\prime}]$ . Since $A[i]=A_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]$ , we have $A[i^{\prime}]\leq A[i]=C[k]$ . By Equation 9, this means $i^{\prime}\in I_{k}$ and $A[i^{\prime}]=A[i]=C[k]$ . Since $f_{x,y}(i^{\prime})\in S_{x,y}$ holds, this contradicts the fact that $i$ is the unique element in $I_{k}$ where $f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}$ , as $i^{\prime}$ is also such an element. ∎By 6.5, as long as we can guarantee that there is a unique witness $i\in I_{k}$ satisfying $f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}$ , we are able to recover it from the result of $\MinWitness(A^{\prime}_{x,y},B^{\prime}_{x,y})$ . The next 6.6 shows this happens with probability $\Omega(1/N^{1/3})$ . Since we initially assumed $|I_{k}|\leq n^{1/3}$ , it thus takes only $\widetilde{O}(N^{1/3})$ repetitions to recover all elements in $I_{k}$ , in total $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3}T(n))$ time as desired. It thus remains to show 6.6 to finish the proof.

#### 6.6.

Let $I_{k}$ be the set of witnesses for $C[k]$ in the Min-Plus Convolution $C=A*B$ where $|I_{k}|\leq n^{1/3}$ , and let $i_{0}\in I_{k}$ be an arbitrary element. Then the probability that $i_{0}$ is the unique element in $I_{k}$ that satisfies $f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}$ is $\Omega(1/N^{1/3})$ .

Note that every $i\in I_{k}$ has the same value $A[i]$ . Let us denote this value by $u$ . Then, for $i\in I_{k}$ , the condition $f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}$ can be equivalently written as

$$ f_{x,y}(i)\in[u\cdot N^{2/3},(u+1)\cdot N^{2/3}). $$

Let $X_{i}$ denote the above event. Note that $\{f_{x,y}\}_{x,y}$ is a nearly $2$ -wise independent hash family. Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left[X_{i_{0}}\wedge\bigwedge_{i\in I_{k}\setminus\{i_{0}\}}\neg X_{i}\right] \displaystyle=\Pr\left[X_{i_{0}}\right]-\Pr\left[X_{i_{0}}\wedge\bigvee_{i\in I_{k}\setminus\{i_{0}\}}X_{i}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{N^{2/3}-1}{N}-\sum_{i\in I_{k}\setminus\{i_{0}\}}\Pr\left[X_{i_{0}}\wedge X_{i}\right] \displaystyle\geq\frac{N^{2/3}-1}{N}-n^{1/3}\cdot\left(\frac{N^{2/3}+1}{N}\right)^{2} \displaystyle=\Omega(N^{-1/3}), $$

where the final step holds because $n\leq N/2$ . ∎

∎

See 1.12

Suppose Min-Witness Convolution can be solved in $O(n^{4/3-\epsilon})$ time for some $\epsilon>0$ by an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ . In order to show this contradicts the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, by Corollary 5.2 with $\gamma=\frac{2}{3}$ , it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for $\MinPlusConvListing(n,n^{2/3}\mid u\leq n^{1/3})$ . Let $(A,B)$ be such a Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance. By Lemma 6.1, we can further assume no elements in $B$ appear more than $n^{2/3+\epsilon/3}$ times. Let $C=A*B$ , which can be computed in $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ time.

For every $b\in[n^{1/3}]$ , we solve a sub-instance between $(A,B_{b})$ , where $B_{b}[j]=0$ if $B[j]=b$ , and $B_{b}[j]=\infty$ otherwise. Using Lemma 6.4 with $\ell=1/3+2\epsilon/3$ , we can list up to $n^{1/3+2\epsilon/3}$ witnesses per output in $C_{b}=A*B_{b}$ . The total cost for calling Lemma 6.4 over $b\in[n^{1/3}]$ is $O(n^{5/3+2\epsilon/3-\epsilon}\cdot n^{1/3})=O(n^{2-\epsilon/3})$ .

If $C_{b}[k]=C[k]-b$ , and Lemma 6.4 lists fewer than $n^{1/3+2\epsilon/3}$ witnesses for $C_{b}[k]$ , then we have listed all witnesses $(i,j)$ satisfying $B[j]=b$ for $C[k]$ . Otherwise, if we have not listed $n^{2/3}$ witnesses for $C[k]$ , we enumerate all non- $\infty$ indices in $B_{b}$ (there can be at most $n^{2/3+\epsilon/3}$ such indices), and check whether it forms a witness for $C[k]$ . The total number of such enumerations is $O(n\cdot n^{1/3-2\epsilon/3})$ , as for each $C[k]$ , one such enumeration increases the number of witnesses found for it by at least $n^{1/3+2\epsilon/3}$ . Hence, the total cost is $O(n\cdot n^{1/3-2\epsilon/3}\cdot n^{2/3+\epsilon/3})=O(n^{2-\epsilon/3})$ , which is truly subquadratic as desired. ∎

## 7 Asymmetric BSG Theorem

In this section, we show an algorithmic version of the Asymmetric BSG Theorem (originally proved by Tao and Vu [52, Section 2.6]), stated as follows. See 2.4

### 7.1 Preliminary Lemmas

Our algorithmic proof of Theorem 2.4 is heavily based on the original proof for the non-algorithmic version by Tao and Vu [52, Section 2.6]. We turn each step into an efficient algorithm using mostly basic ideas.

We start with the following definition from [52, Definition 2.32]:

#### 7.1Symmetry Sets.

For $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and $0<\alpha\leq 1$ , we define the symmetry set

$$ \Sym(A;\alpha)=\{x\in A-A:r_{A-A}(x)\geq\alpha|A|\}. $$

Note that $0\in\Sym(A;\alpha)$ and $\Sym(A;\alpha)=-\Sym(A;\alpha)$ . Moreover, it holds that

$$ |\Sym(A;\alpha)|\leq\frac{|A|}{\alpha}, $$

which follows readily from $\sum_{x\in A-A}r_{A-A}(x)=|A|^{2}$ . In the notation from before one can equivalently express the symmetry set as a set of popular differences, $\Sym(A;\alpha)=\Pop(A,-A;\alpha|A|)$ .

We need the following lemma corresponding to [52, Lemma 2.34].

#### 7.2Dyadic Pigeonhole Principle.

Let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $A,D\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ be such that

$$ \sum_{x\in D}r_{A-A}(x)\geq\alpha|A|^{2}. $$

Then there is a subset $D^{\prime}\subseteq D$ such that, for every $x\in D^{\prime}$ ,

$$ r_{A-A}(x)\geq\Omega\left\lparen\frac{\alpha}{1+\log\frac{1}{\alpha}+\log(1+\frac{|D|}{|A|})}\cdot\frac{|A|^{2}}{|D^{\prime}|}\right\rparen. $$

Moreover, there is a randomized algorithm that, given $A$ , $\alpha$ and $D$ , computes such a set $D^{\prime}$ in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|D|/\alpha)$ .

We first call Lemma 2.5 on the sets $A,-A,D$ with parameter $\epsilon=\min(\frac{\alpha|A|}{8|D|},1)$ to approximate the multiplicities $r_{A-A}(x)$ for all $x\in D$ by $0\leq\tilde{r}(x)\leq|A|$ within additive error

$$ |r_{A-A}(x)-\tilde{r}(x)|\leq\epsilon|A|=\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{8|D|}. $$

Let

$$ D^{*}=\left\{x\in D:\tilde{r}(x)\geq\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{4|D|}\right\}. $$

This set is chosen so that for all $x\in D^{*}$ we have $r_{A-A}(x)\geq\tilde{r}(x)/2$ . Further observe that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{x\in D^{*}}\tilde{r}(x) \displaystyle\geq\sum_{x\in D}\tilde{r}(x)-\sum_{x\in D\setminus D^{*}}\tilde{r}(x) \displaystyle\geq\sum_{x\in D}\tilde{r}(x)-|D|\cdot\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{4|D|} \displaystyle\geq\sum_{x\in D}r_{A-A}(x)-|D|\cdot\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{8|D|}-|D|\cdot\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{4|D|} \displaystyle\geq\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{2}. $$

Now let $L$ be the smallest integer with $2^{-L}<\frac{\alpha|A|}{2|D|}$ , and consider the partition of $D^{*}$ into $D_{1},\dots,D_{L}$ defined by

$$ D_{\ell}=\left\{x\in D^{*}:\frac{|A|}{2^{\ell}}<\tilde{r}(x)\leq\frac{|A|}{2^{\ell-1}}\right\}. $$

By the pigeonhole principle at least one part $1\leq\ell\leq L$ satisfies

$$ \sum_{x\in D_{\ell}}\tilde{r}(x)\geq\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{2L}; $$

take that part and report $D^{\prime}=D_{\ell}$ . Indeed, each $x\in D_{\ell}$ satisfies

$$ r_{A-A}(x)\geq\frac{\tilde{r}(x)}{2}\geq\frac{|A|}{2^{\ell+1}}\geq\frac{\sum_{x\in D_{\ell}}\tilde{r}(x)}{4|D_{\ell}|}\geq\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{8L|D_{\ell}|}, $$

which is as claimed, recalling that $L\leq 1+\log\frac{1}{\alpha}+\log(1+\frac{|D|}{|A|})$ .

Finally, consider the running time. Lemma 2.5 takes time $\widetilde{O}(|A|/\epsilon+|D|)=\widetilde{O}(|A|+|D|/\alpha)$ . All subsequent steps, including the construction of $D^{*}$ , its partitioning, and selecting the relevant part $D_{\ell}$ , run in linear time $O(|D|)$ . ∎

We also rely on the following lemma, which is a combination of [52, Lemma 2.33] and [52, Lemma 2.34].

#### 7.3.

Let $0<\alpha\leq 1$ and let $A,S$ be sets with $S\subseteq\Sym(A;\alpha)$ . Then:

$$ \lvert\{(s_{1},s_{2})\in S^{2}:s_{1}-s_{2}\in\Sym(A;\alpha^{2}/2)\}\rvert\geq\frac{\alpha^{2}|S|^{2}}{2}. $$

Supposing otherwise,

$$ \displaystyle E(A,S) \displaystyle=\sum_{s_{1},s_{2}\in S}r_{A-A}(s_{1}-s_{2}) \displaystyle<\frac{\alpha^{2}|S|^{2}}{2}\cdot|A|+|S|^{2}\cdot\frac{\alpha^{2}|A|}{2} \displaystyle=\alpha^{2}|S|^{2}|A|. $$

But at the same time, by Cauchy–Schwarz,

$$ \displaystyle E(A,S) \displaystyle\geq\sum_{a\in A}r_{A+S}(a)^{2} \displaystyle\geq\frac{\left\lparen\sum_{a\in A}r_{A+S}(a)\right\rparen^{2}}{|A|} \displaystyle=\frac{\left\lparen\sum_{s\in S}r_{A-A}(s)\right\rparen^{2}}{|A|} \displaystyle\geq\frac{(|S|\cdot\alpha|A|)^{2}}{|A|} \displaystyle=\alpha^{2}|S|^{2}|A|, $$

which shows the desired contradiction. ∎

### 7.2 Existential Proof

In this subsection we finally prove the existential statement of Theorem 2.4. Recall that we start from integer sets $A,B$ with energy

$$ E(A,B)\geq\alpha|A|^{2}|B|. $$

The proof can conceptually be split into four steps. In the first step we will successively replace $A$ by “smoother” sets $A_{1},A_{2},\dots$ that admit more additive structure. As an instructive example, consider the set $B=\{1,\dots,|B|\}$ and let $A$ be a random subset of $B$ . When $B$ is large compared to $A$ , $A$ essentially admits no additive structure at all. We will therefore replace $A$ by smoother sets (think of $A-A,2A-2A,\dots$ ) converging to the highly structured set $B$ . Once we reach a set that is sufficiently structured, in the second step we apply the symmetric BSG theorem to identify a large low-doubling subset $H$ . In the third step we unroll the iterative smoothing procedure to relate $H$ to the initial set $A$ . In the fourth step we relate $H$ to $B$ .

Following [52], we introduce a useful piece of notation. We write $f=O_{j}(g)$ if there exists a positive constant $C(j)$ (that only depends on $j$ ) such that

$$ f\leq C(j)\cdot\alpha^{-C(j)}\cdot\left\lparen 1+\log\frac{|B|}{|A|}\right\rparen^{C(j)}\cdot g; $$

that is, the $O_{j}$ notation hides constant factors, polynomial factors in $1/\alpha$ , and polylogarithmic factors in $|B|/|A|$ . Similarly define $f=\Omega_{j}(g)$ .

#### Step 1: Iteratively Smoothing $A$

Let $J=J(\epsilon)$ be a constant to be fixed later. Let $\alpha_{1}=\alpha/2$ and recursively define $\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{J}$ by $\alpha_{j+1}=\alpha_{j}^{2}/2$ . Note that $\alpha_{1}>\dots>\alpha_{J}>0$ and $\alpha_{j}=\Omega_{j}(1)$ . We will inductively construct a sequence of sets $A_{0},A_{1},\dots,A_{J}$ with the following properties:

- (i) for all $1\leq j\leq J$ , $A_{j}\subseteq\Sym(B;\alpha_{j})$ ,

- (ii) for all $0\leq j<J$ and all $x\in A_{j+1}$ , $r_{A_{j}-A_{j}}(x)\geq\Omega_{j}\lparen|A_{j}|^{2}/|A_{j+1}|\rparen$ ,

- (iii) for all $0\leq j\leq J$ , $|A_{j}|=\Omega_{j}(|A|)$ .

In fact, Property 3 is always implied by Property 2: If $\sum_{x\in A_{j+1}}r_{A_{j}-A_{j}}(x)\geq\Omega_{j}(|A_{j}|^{2})$ , then we must have $|A_{j+1}|\geq\Omega_{j}(|A_{j}|)$ , and then Property 3 follows by induction. For this reason we will only ensure Properties 1 and 2 in the following construction.

The base case is concerned with the construction of $A_{0}$ and $A_{1}$ . We trivially take $A_{0}=A$ . To construct $A_{1}$ , first observe that

$$ \displaystyle E(A,B) \displaystyle=\sum_{a_{1},a_{2}\in A}r_{B-B}(a_{1}-a_{2}) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{a_{1},a_{2}\in A}\frac{\alpha|B|}{2}+\lvert\{(a_{1},a_{2})\in A^{2}:a_{1}-a_{2}\in\Sym(B;\alpha/2)\}\rvert\cdot|B|. $$

In particular, recalling that $E(A,B)\geq\alpha|A|^{2}|B|$ , and letting $D=\Sym(B;\alpha/2)$ , we must have

$$ \sum_{x\in D}r_{A-A}(x)\geq\frac{\alpha|A|^{2}}{2}. $$

Hence, Lemma 7.2 yields a set $A_{1}\subseteq D=\Sym(B;\alpha/2)$ that directly satisfies both Properties 1 and 2.

Now focus on the inductive case, i.e., let $j\geq 1$ , assume that $A_{j}$ has already been constructed, and focus on the construction of $A_{j+1}$ . By 1 we have $A_{j}\subseteq\Sym(B;\alpha_{j})$ . Apply Lemma 7.3 with $\alpha_{j}$ and sets $B,A_{j}$ , yielding that

$$ \lvert\{(a_{1},a_{2})\in A_{j}^{2}:a_{1}-a_{2}\in\Sym(B;\alpha_{j}^{2}/2)\}\rvert\geq\frac{\alpha_{j}^{2}|A_{j}|^{2}}{2}. $$

Next, apply Lemma 7.2 with parameter $\alpha_{j+1}=\alpha_{j}^{2}/2$ on the sets $A_{j},\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})$ to construct a set $A_{j+1}\subseteq\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})$ satisfying, for all $x\in A_{j+1}$ ,

$$ r_{A_{j}-A_{j}}(x)=\Omega\left\lparen\frac{\alpha_{j}}{1+\log\frac{1}{\alpha_{j}}+\log(1+\frac{|\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})|}{|A_{j}|})}\cdot\frac{|A_{j}|^{2}}{|A_{j+1}|}\right\rparen=\Omega_{j}\left\lparen\frac{|A_{j}|^{2}}{|A_{j+1}|}\right\rparen. $$

In the last step we used that $|A_{j}|=\Omega_{j}(|A|)$ (by 3) and $|\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})|\leq|B|/\alpha_{j+1}$ ; taken together these imply that $\log(1+|\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})|/|A_{j}|)$ can be hidden in the $\Omega_{j}$ notation. Evidently, the set $A_{j+1}$ satisfies both Properties 1 and 2, completing the construction.

#### Step 2: Constructing $H$ by the BSG Theorem

Take $0\leq j<J$ minimizing $|A_{j+1}|/|A_{j}|$ . Recall that $|A_{0}|=|A|$ and that $|A_{J}|\leq|\Sym(B;\alpha_{J})|\leq|B|/\alpha_{J}=O_{J}(|B|)$ by Property 1. Thus, writing $L=1+|B|/|A|$ , we must have

$$ |A_{j+1}|=O_{J}\left\lparen L^{1/J}\cdot|A_{j}|\right\rparen. $$

Moreover, Property 2 implies that

$$ \displaystyle E(A_{j}) \displaystyle=\sum_{x\in A_{j}-A_{j}}r_{A_{j}-A_{j}}(x)^{2} \displaystyle\geq\sum_{x\in A_{j+1}}r_{A_{j}-A_{j}}(x)^{2} \displaystyle=\Omega_{j}\left\lparen\frac{|A_{j}|^{4}}{|A_{j+1}|}\right\rparen \displaystyle=\Omega_{J}\left\lparen\frac{|A_{j}|^{3}}{L^{1/J}}\right\rparen. $$

In this situation, the symmetric BSG theorem (Theorem 2.3) applies, yielding some $K_{j}=O_{J}(L^{O(1/J)})$ and a set $H$ with

$$ |H|\leq K_{j}|A_{j}|, $$

and

$$ |H+H|\leq K_{j}|H|, $$

and

$$ |A_{j}\cap H|\geq\frac{|A_{j}|}{K_{j}}. $$

Equation 11 is claimed as in the theorem statement (once we fix the parameter $J$ ). Equations 10 and 12 involve $A_{j}$ rather than $A$ ; in the following we show that these imply similar statements for $A$ .

#### Step 3: Relating $H$ to $A$

To relate $H$ to $A$ , we traverse the sets $A=A_{0},A_{1},\dots,A_{j}$ backwards. More precisely, we deduce from $|A_{j}\cap(H+x_{j})|\geq|A_{j}|/K_{j}$ that $|A_{j-1}\cap(H+x_{j-1})|\geq|A_{j-1}|/K_{j-1}$ , for some shifts $x_{j-1}$ and parameters $K_{j-1}$ (we have $x_{j}=0$ ). Indeed, assuming $|A_{j}\cap(H+x_{j})|\geq|A_{j}|/K_{j}$ , Property 2 implies that

$$ \lvert\{(a_{1},a_{2})\in A_{j-1}^{2}:a_{1}-a_{2}\in(H+x_{j})\}\rvert\geq\Omega_{j}\left\lparen\frac{|A_{j-1}|^{2}}{K_{j}}\right\rparen, $$

or equivalently,

$$ \sum_{a\in A_{j-1}}|A_{j-1}\cap(H+x_{j}+a)|\geq\Omega_{j}\left\lparen\frac{|A_{j-1}|^{2}}{K_{j}}\right\rparen. $$

In particular, there is some $a$ such that $|A_{j-1}\cap(H+x_{j}+a)|\geq\Omega_{j}(|A_{j-1}|/K_{j})$ . Choosing $x_{j-1}=x_{j}+a$ and $K_{j-1}=O_{j}(K_{j})$ , the claim follows. By induction we learn that

$$ |A\cap(H+x_{0})|\geq\frac{|A|}{K_{0}}, $$

for some translate $x_{0}$ and some parameter

$$ K_{0}=O_{j}(K_{j})=O_{J}(L^{O(1/J)}). $$

Equation 13 is exactly as claimed in the theorem statement, when shifting $H$ by $x_{0}$ .

#### Step 4: Relating $H$ to $B$

We finally relate $H$ to $B$ . Combining Property 1 with Equations 10 and 12 implies that

$$ |H\cap\Sym(B;\alpha_{j})|\geq\frac{|H|}{K_{j}^{2}}. $$

In particular, by definition of $\Sym(B;\alpha_{j})$ we have

$$ \lvert\{(b,h)\in B\times H:b+h\in B\}\rvert\geq\frac{\alpha_{j}}{K_{j}^{2}}\cdot|B|\,|H|. $$

Let $\Lambda\subseteq B$ be a random subset, sampled with rate $p=\min(1,4K_{j}^{2}/(\alpha_{j}|H|))$ . Then, with constant probability,

$$ |B\cap(H+\Lambda)|\geq\frac{\alpha_{j}}{4K_{j}^{2}}\cdot|B|. $$

To see this, call an element $b\in B$ relevant if

$$ r_{B+H}(b)\geq\frac{\alpha_{j}}{2K_{j}^{2}}\cdot|H|. $$

Equation 14 entails that there must be at least $\alpha_{j}/2K_{j}^{2}\cdot|B|$ relevant elements. But each relevant item is not covered in $H+\Lambda$ with probability at most $(1-p)^{\frac{\alpha_{j}}{2K_{j}^{2}}\cdot|H|}$ . When $p=1$ , this trivially equals $0$ ; otherwise,

$$ (1-p)^{\frac{\alpha_{j}}{2K_{j}^{2}}\cdot|H|}\leq\exp(-p\cdot\frac{\alpha_{j}}{2K_{j}^{2}}\cdot|H|)\leq\exp(-2)<\frac{1}{4}. $$

By Markov’s inequality, with probability at least $1/2$ , at least half the relevant elements are covered by $H+\Lambda$ . This proves Equation 15. At the same time, $\Lambda$ satisfies the following size bound with high probability:

$$ |\Lambda|\leq O\left\lparen\frac{K_{j}^{2}}{\alpha_{j}}\cdot\frac{|B|}{|H|}\right\rparen. $$

#### Wrapping Up

All in all, Equations 11, 16, 13 and 15 are as claimed in Theorem 2.4; it only remains to choose appropriate parameters. All these equations have an overhead of the form $O_{J}(L^{O(1/J)})$ , i.e.,

$$ C(J)\cdot\alpha^{-C(J)}\cdot L^{C_{0}/J}\cdot(\log L)^{C(J)}, $$

for some absolute constant $C_{0}$ and some constant $C(J)$ depending on $J$ . Choosing $J>C_{0}/\epsilon$ , this overhead indeed takes the form

$$ K=O_{\epsilon}(\alpha^{-O_{\epsilon}(1)}L^{\epsilon}). $$

The proof of Theorem 2.4 is complete.

### 7.3 Efficient Algorithm

In this section we finally argue that the previous proof can be implemented by an efficient algorithm, running in time $\widetilde{O}((|A|+|B|)K)$ for some $K\leq O_{\epsilon}(\alpha^{-O_{\epsilon}(1)}L^{\epsilon})$ . To this end, we revisit the four steps from before and comment on their implementations.

#### Step 1: Iteratively Smoothing $A$

In the first step we explicitly compute the sets $A_{1},\dots,A_{J}$ . This step is already almost completely algorithmic. Each set $A_{j+1}$ is constructed by one call to Lemma 7.2 on input $A_{j}$ and $D=\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})$ ; the only problem is that we do not have access to $\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})$ . Instead, we will compute some superset

$$ \Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})\subseteq D\subseteq\Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1}/2) $$

by Lemma 3.3 in time $\widetilde{O}(|B|/\alpha_{j+1})$ . This leaves the correctness unchanged. The running time of Lemma 7.2 can then be bounded by

$$ \widetilde{O}\left\lparen|A_{j}|+\frac{|D|}{\alpha_{j+1}}\right\rparen=\widetilde{O}\left\lparen\frac{|B|}{\alpha_{j+1}^{2}}\right\rparen. $$

The total time of step 1 is dominated by the final iteration, $\widetilde{O}(|B|/\alpha_{J}^{2})$ , which is within the budget.

#### Step 2: Constructing $H$ by the BSG Theorem

In step 2 we first identify the index $j$ minimizing $|A_{j+1}|/|A_{j}|$ . Since we have computed the sets $A_{1},\dots,A_{J}$ explicitly, this can be done in linear time. Then we apply the BSG theorem (Theorem 2.3) to the set $A_{j}$ to construct $H$ . This runs in time $\widetilde{O}(|A_{j}|K_{j})$ , for some $K_{j}=O_{J}(L^{O(1/J)})$ as before. Again, recalling that $|A_{j}|\leq|B|/\alpha_{j}$ by Property 3, this is within the claimed time budget.

#### Step 3: Relating $H$ to $A$

The only data that we need to compute in this step is the shift $x_{0}$ satisfying Equation 13, i.e.,

$$ |A\cap(H+x_{0})|\geq\frac{|A|}{K_{0}}. $$

In fact, we settle for a slightly weaker condition. Namely, observe that this shift $x_{0}$ is equivalently an element of $\Pop(A,-H;|A|/K_{0})$ . Hence, to find $x_{0}$ we may run Lemma 3.3 to compute a set sandwiched between $\Pop(A,-H;|A|/K_{0})$ and $\Pop(A,-H;|A|/2K_{0})$ , and pick any element $x_{0}$ from that set. By definition, that element satisfies

$$ |A\cap(H+x_{0})|\geq\frac{|A|}{2K_{0}}. $$

We may increase $K_{0}$ to $2K_{0}$ without any harm, and then $x_{0}$ is as claimed in Equation 13.

The running time is dominated by the call to Lemma 3.3 in time $\widetilde{O}(|H|K_{0})$ . By Equation 10 and Property 3 this is at most $\widetilde{O}(|A_{j}|K_{j}K_{0})=\widetilde{O}(|B|K_{j}K_{0}/\alpha_{j})$ , which is within the budget.

#### Step 4: Relating $H$ to $B$

The final step only involves the construction of $\Lambda$ . Recall that $\Lambda$ is constructed as a random subset of $B$ , sampled with an appropriate rate $p$ . We have argued that with constant probability, the size $|B\cap(H+\Lambda)|$ is at least as large as claimed in Equation 15. The only modification in our algorithm is to amplify the success probability. That is, we sample $R=\Theta(\log|B|)$ sets $\Lambda_{1},\dots,\Lambda_{R}$ , compute the sumsets $H+\Lambda_{1},\dots,H+\Lambda_{R}$ by brute-force, and report the set $\Lambda_{r}$ maximizing $|B\cap(H+\Lambda_{r})|$ . With high probability that choice satisfies Equation 15. Moreover, with high probability all sets $\Lambda_{1},\dots,\Lambda_{R}$ simultaneously satisfy the size bound from Equation 16,

$$ |\Lambda_{1}|,\dots,|\Lambda_{R}|\leq O\left\lparen\frac{K_{j}^{2}}{\alpha_{j}}\cdot\frac{|B|}{|H|}\right\rparen. $$

The running time of step 4 is therefore bounded by

$$ O\left\lparen\sum_{r=1}^{R}\left\lparen|B|+|H|\,|\Lambda_{r}|\right\rparen\right\rparen=\widetilde{O}\left\lparen\frac{K_{j}^{2}}{\alpha_{j}}\cdot|B|\right\rparen. $$

This is within the claimed time budget.

N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) is a probable human carcinogen found in contaminated pharmaceuticals and drinking water, yet the impact of age on NDMA susceptibility remains poorly understood. Using DNA repair-deﬁcient (Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-) and wild-type mice, we systematically compare the effects of NDMA exposure in juveniles and adults. Juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice are profoundly more vulnerable, exhibiting persistent DNA damage, inﬂammation, and mutations that lead to liver pathology and tumorigenesis, particularly in males. Adults, by comparison, are resistant to NDMA. Wild-type mice show similar, attenuated trends. NDMA-induced DNA adduct levels are comparable across age groups, implicating proliferation-dependent responses to adducts, rather than adduct formation, as the primary driver of age-related risk. Supporting this mechanism, triiodothyronine-stimulated cell proliferation in adults partially recapitulates juvenile sensitivity, linking cell division to NDMA genotoxicity. Our ﬁndings identify developmental stage, sex, and DNA repair capacity as key modiﬁers of NDMA-induced carcinogenesis, with potential implications for environmental risk assessment and regulatory policy.

While children and adolescents account for a quarter of the population, our understanding of their potential heightened risk from environmental carcinogens remains limited1. In this study, we investigated the role of age as a susceptibility factor to N-nitrosamine exposure. N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA), a probable human carcinogen, exempliﬁes this concern2. NDMA has been detected in various sources,

including food, drinking water, cigarette smoke, and pharmaceuticals. Although epidemiological evidence in humans remains limited, there are studies that link NDMA exposure to elevated risks of bladder, stomach, prostate, and liver cancers, as well as leukemia and multiple myeloma2,3. Understanding the mechanisms underlying age-dependent responses to NDMA in experimental models is therefore critical. NDMA exposure through inhalation, ingestion, or injection increases the incidence of liver, lung, and kidney tumors in rodents2. The adverse health effects of NDMA exposure in animals are most severe in the liver and include centrilobular necrosis, hemorrhage, ﬁbrosis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and cancer. NDMA’s mutagenicity arises from its metabolism by cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1), which generates the highly reactive methyldiazonium ion. This intermediate methylates DNA to form mutagenic adducts such as O6- methylguanine (O6MeG) and 3-methyladenine (3MeA). If unrepaired, these adducts can induce mutations, toxicity, and inﬂammation, thus promoting carcinogenesis and aging2,4–10. O6MeG is restored to guanine through direct reversal by the suicide protein O6-methylguanine- DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), while the remediation of 3MeA via base excision repair is initiated by 3-alkyladenine DNA glycosylase (AAG/MPG). Mice lacking MGMT or AAG exhibit heightened susceptibility to NDMA-induced genotoxicity and tumorigenesis2,4–10. In MGMT knockout mice, O6MeG mispairs with thymine during replication, while in AAG knockouts, 3MeA is bypassed with errors, both increasing point mutations4–10. Mismatch repair of O6MeG/T can generate singlestranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps and double-strand breaks (DSBs), and replication-blocking adducts like 3MeA can lead to replication fork stress4,5,7–12. These lesions may be resolved via homologous recombination, which can cause large-scale sequence rearrangements including deletions, translocations, or loss of heterozygosity, all of which are commonly associated with cancer4,7. Collectively, these mechanisms illustrate the mutagenic potential of unrepaired NDMA-induced adducts. The downstream consequences of NDMA-induced DNA adduct formation extend beyond mutagenesis. Persistent mismatches, ssDNA gaps, stalled forks, and DSBs activate DNA damage response (DDR) pathways, triggering both cell death and compensatory tissue regeneration11–15. These DDR pathways concurrently stimulate inﬂammatory responses and interferon signaling, driving the activation of hepatic progenitor cells and resident macrophages, as well as the recruitment of circulating immune cells to injury sites. While these processes initially function to promote repair, chronic activation fosters tumorigenesis by enhancing cellular proliferation and survival signaling, thus creating a microenvironment conducive to mutation accumulation14–17. Although NDMA toxicity has been widely studied in animal models, the inﬂuence of age on the severity of NDMA-induced DNA damage, inﬂammation, mutagenesis, and long-term liver pathology remains largely unexplored2. To address this knowledge gap, we exposed both juvenile and adult mice to NDMA via drinking water and systematically evaluated molecular, cellular, and tissue-level responses. We utilized mice lacking both AAG and MGMT genes (Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-) as a mechanistic model that serves several critical purposes: (1) both MGMT and AAG exhibit substantial interindividual variation in humans2,4,7, making the model relevant to studies of geneenvironment interactions; (2) the model ampliﬁes NDMA-induced responses, thus requiring fewer animals; and (3) it provides mechanistic insights into how DNA repair capacity and age interact to inﬂuence carcinogenic outcomes. We selected a relatively high drinking water dose of 5 ppm NDMA to ensure measurable biological effects within the two-week exposure period and to align with established toxicological studies2. Using this approach, we show that age is a critical determinant of the NDMA response, with younger mice exhibiting substantially greater DNA damage, interferon-mediated inﬂammation, mutations, and liver pathology. While this age-dependent susceptibility was most

pronounced in DNA repair-deﬁcient mice, a similar effect was also observed in WT animals, demonstrating developmental stage as a key risk factor even when repair pathways are intact. Importantly, neither CYP2E1 expression nor DNA adduct levels varied signiﬁcantly by age, suggesting that age-related risk reﬂects the proliferation-dependent processing of adducts rather than differences in metabolism. This conclusion is supported by the increased susceptibility to NDMAinduced genotoxicity in adult mice treated with proliferationstimulating triiodothyronine (T3). We also observed sex-dependent differences, consistent with known sexual dimorphism in liver biology. By revealing how age, DNA repair capacity, and sex interact to shape the response to a relevant environmental carcinogen, our study provides new insight into the mechanisms underlying early life vulnerability and highlights the importance of considering developmental stage in toxicological assessment.

Results Enhanced juvenile genotoxicity is independent of DNA adduct levels To investigate how age modulates the genotoxicity of NDMA, we exposed DNA repair-deﬁcient (Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-) mice to 5 ppm NDMA in drinking water for two weeks, starting at postnatal day 21 (juveniles) or day 90 (adults) (Fig. 1a, b). Formalin-ﬁxed liver sections were then analyzed for H2AX phosphorylated at Ser139 (γH2AX), a marker of replication stress and DNA DSBs18. Juvenile mice exhibited a striking increase in γH2AX levels immediately following the 14-day NDMA exposure period (14 + 0 d), an effect entirely absent in adults (Fig. 1c). Importantly, γH2AX persisted in juvenile livers 10 days post-exposure but remained undetectable in adults (Fig. 1d). Western blot analysis reinforced these age-speciﬁc disparities, revealing signiﬁcantly elevated γH2AX only in younger animals after NDMA treatment (Fig. 1e). To conﬁrm that this age-dependent response was independent of exposure route, we also administered NDMA via intraperitoneal injection (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Consistently, juvenile mice showed a stronger γH2AX response by both histology and western blot following direct exposure (Supplementary Fig. 1b, c). This robust, agedependent induction of γH2AX across exposure routes highlights the particular vulnerability of juvenile mice to unresolved replication stress and DSBs. Stressed replication forks and DNA strand breaks can trigger DDRs13. To further explore, we analyzed p53 phosphorylated at Ser15 (p-p53), a central effector in DDR pathways, which was signiﬁcantly increased in juveniles treated with 5 ppm NDMA but not in adults (Fig. 1e). Furthermore, NDMA exposure in younger mice resulted in increased total p53 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). p53 activation can lead to increased transcription of p21, promoting cell cycle arrest13. Western blot results showed p21 induction exclusively in juveniles (Fig. 1e). This p21-mediated cell cycle arrest in response to NDMA exposure provides extended time for DNA repair processes, such as homologous recombination. RAD51, critical for homologous recombination repair of DNA DSBs and replication fork processing, was upregulated only in juveniles (Fig. 1e)13. Collectively, these ﬁndings demonstrate that younger mice mount a heightened, age-dependent DDR to NDMA. Disparities in DDRs may stem from differences in adductlevels. To explore this, we quantiﬁed the levels of O6MeG and 3MeA by mass spectrometry. Both adducts were substantially increased in juveniles and adults after NDMA exposure (Fig. 1f), but no signiﬁcant differences were detected between age groups. This suggests that upstream processes such as NDMA metabolism and adduct formation are comparable across ages. Supporting this view, CYP2E1 protein levels were similar in untreated juvenile and adult control mice before and after the exposure timeline (Fig. 1g). Thus, the pronounced sensitivity of juveniles to NDMA-induced DDRs occurs independently of adduct levels. Having established that age strikingly inﬂuences the cellular response to NDMA-induced DNA damage, we next examined how

Prolonged inﬂammation and compensatory proliferation in juveniles DNA damage and responses activate interferon signaling and downstream immune pathways, which, under chronic conditions, can establish a self-perpetuating cycle of tissue injury14,17. As such, we assessed STAT1 phosphorylated at Tyr701 (pSTAT1), a central marker of the interferon response19. A signiﬁcant increase in pSTAT1 was

observed only in juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice exposed to NDMA (Fig. 2a), along with elevated total STAT1 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Adults, by contrast, exhibited no signiﬁcant changes in pSTAT1 or STAT1. Sustained interferon activation through STAT1 in response to DNA damage can lead to STAT3 activation (pSTAT3; Tyr705), forming a negative feedback loop that regulates inﬂammation and DDRs14,19,20. pSTAT3 was upregulated only in juvenile mice (Fig. 2a), reﬂecting unresolved inﬂammation. In line with this expectation, juvenile mice displayed moderately increased histiocytic and lymphocytic cell foci following NDMA exposure, an effect that was not as prominent in adults (Fig. 2b). Although inﬂammation in juveniles largely resolved by 10 days postexposure, a trend persisted (Supplementary Fig. 3a). To further investigate the mechanisms underlying the observed pathology, we examined molecular markers of immune cells. NDMA exposure in juvenile mice led to a signiﬁcant upregulation of immune cell markers CD3e (Fig. 2a) and CD11C (Supplementary Fig. 2a), indicating stimulation and recruitment of immune cells to the liver21. These immune responses were absent in adult mice, highlighting the unique vulnerability of younger animals. The recruitment and activation of immune cells drive the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), a response particularly evident in juveniles, as shown by the signiﬁcant upregulation of antioxidant enzyme HO-1 (Fig. 2a)22. This effect was also observed following intraperitoneal injection exclusively in juveniles, supporting the pronounced redox imbalance induced by NDMA in younger mice (Supplementary Fig. 1c). Excessive RONS levels can lead to hepatocellular degeneration, which was signiﬁcantly more severe in juveniles treated with 5 ppm NDMA than in adults, as evidenced by the distinct multifocal, centrilobular hepatocellular degeneration (Fig. 2b)16. This injury persisted at 10 days and even 3 months postexposure in juveniles (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b), indicating long-term hepatic damage in younger mice. To further dissect the consequences of NDMA-induced DNA adducts and associated inﬂammation, we analyzed markers of cell death across age groups. Western blot analysis demonstrated that a key apoptosis marker, cleaved caspase-3, was increased only in juvenile mice following NDMA exposure, but not adults (Fig. 2c)23. While single-cell necrosis was not immediately apparent (Fig. 2d), it became signiﬁcantly elevated only in juveniles by 10 days post treatment (Fig. 2e)24. These results indicate that younger mice sustain prolonged and multifaceted hepatocellular damage after NDMA exposure, with apoptosis dominating acutely and necrosis emerging during recovery. Following organ damage and inﬂammation, tissues undergo regenerative cell proliferation14–16. Liver regeneration, as measured by Ki67 staining, was heightened in juveniles (Fig. 2f)25. Western blot analysis conﬁrmed increased expression of proliferation markers MCM2 and PCNA speciﬁcally in juvenile mice (Supplementary Fig. 2a). This proliferative response remained elevated for at least 10 days postexposure (Fig. 2g), indicating ongoing regeneration in younger mice. In adults, Ki67 levels remained unchanged, emphasizing a lack of compensatory proliferation. When NDMA was administered via intraperitoneal injection, juveniles consistently exhibited cell death (cleaved caspase-3; Supplementary Fig. 1c) and proliferation (Ki67 and PCNA; Supplementary Fig. 1b, c), mirroring responses seen with drinking water exposure. These ﬁndings reveal that interferon-driven immune activation and oxidative stress promotes age-dependent liver injury and regenerative proliferation in juveniles.

Younger mice display persistent transcriptomic dysregulation The liver’s capacity for regeneration and detoxiﬁcation is governed by a complex network of DNA repair, cell cycle, and immune pathways, which is largely shaped by changes in gene expression14–16. To uncover how developmental stage shapes the hepatic response to NDMA, we analyzed the transcriptome in juvenile and adult Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice immediately after exposure and during recovery (Supplementary Data 1). Juvenile mice demonstrated an 11-fold increase in the number of signiﬁcantly upregulated or downregulated genes compared to adults (Fig. 3a), highlighting a much broader transcriptional disruption in younger animals. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of juveniles revealed clear segregation of NDMA-treated and untreated samples (Fig. 3b), with global gene expression patterns primarily deﬁned by NDMA exposure rather than sex. Even after a 10-day recovery, juveniles retained substantial gene expression changes, whereas adults exhibited only minor alterations (Fig. 3c). These ﬁndings reveal the magnitude of age-dependent transcriptomic reprogramming in response to NDMA. Consistent with protein-level data (Fig. 1e), juveniles exhibited robust upregulation of DDR genes, including Cdkn1a (p21), Ccng1, Ddit4l, and Pttg1, all persisting through the 10-day recovery (Fig. 3d)13,26–28. In contrast, adults showed induction of only Cdkn1a (p21) immediately following exposure, albeit 2-fold less than juveniles (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Data 1), with no corresponding, statistically signiﬁcant increase in protein levels (Fig. 1e). Pathway enrichment further revealed the exclusive activation of DDR-related pathways (p53, UV Response Up) in juveniles, with the p53 pathway continuing 10 days post-exposure (Fig. 3e). Adults showed no comparable pathway activation, underscoring their resilience. DDR orchestrates cell fate decisions, and in juveniles, we observed concurrent activation of mTORC1 signaling, a key regulator of growth and metabolism14, and apoptotic pathways (Fig. 3e). This simultaneous engagement of proliferative and cell death mechanisms in response to unresolved DNA damage uniquely characterizes the juvenile hepatic response, and is further supported by protein expression and histological analyses (Fig. 2c–g and Supplementary Fig. 2a). DNA damage and response pathways are well-established activators of innate immune signaling and subsequent inﬂammation17. In juveniles, NDMA exposure led to a signiﬁcant upregulation of immune modulators, including Stat1, Cd63, Iﬁ27, Igtp, Iigp1, Serpina3n, Ly6e, and Mbl2 (Fig. 3d)19,29,30. While expression of all of these immune-related genes remained elevated in juveniles for at least 10 days post-exposure, only one gene was induced at both timepoints in adults. Inﬂammatory processes are also known to transcriptionally suppress Cyp2e131, the primary enzyme mediating NDMA bioactivation, which was notably downregulated exclusively in younger mice even at 10 days post-exposure (Fig. 3d). This suppression likely reﬂects robust inﬂammation and stress signaling following NDMA exposure, consistent with established mechanisms in which activation of pathways such as NF-κB leads to decreased hepatic Cyp2e1 expression during liver injury and immune activation32. Age-dependent mutagenesis and clonal expansion in younger mice NDMA-induced DNA adducts can generate both point and largescale mutations, which are replication-dependent and may be inﬂuenced by age4–7. To assess age-related effects on NDMA mutagenesis in Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice, we employed two complementary transgenic reporter systems: the gptΔ transgene, which detects point mutations via 6-thioguanine resistance in E. coli (Fig. 4a), and the RaDR transgene, which identiﬁes large-scale sequence rearrangements through restoration of EGFP expression following erroneous homologous recombination (Fig. 4b)5,6. These assays together enable precise discrimination between base-level mutations and extensive genomic alterations induced by NDMA, providing a comprehensive assessment of mutagenic mechanisms and their modulation by age. Replication-dependent misinsertions are well-established drivers of point mutations caused by NDMA exposure4–7. Using the gptΔ assay, we observed that juvenile mice exhibited substantially higher point mutation frequencies compared to adults when analyzed 3 months post-exposure (Fig. 4c). While adult mice showed no statistically signiﬁcant increase relative to controls, an upward trend suggested residual mutagenic activity. Given the severe mutational burden in the highly proliferative livers of younger mice, these ﬁndings support DNA replication as a central mechanism facilitating misinsertions and subsequent point mutations. Genotoxic ssDNA gaps, replication stress, and DSBs can induce large-scale mutations via misaligned homologous recombination events, which we evaluated using our RaDR-GFP mouse model4,7,43. Fresh liver tissue was imaged for levels of RaDR foci, indicative of recombinant mutant cells, at multiple timepoints up to 10-11 months

post-exposure (Fig. 4d). Strikingly, age had a profound inﬂuence on NDMA-induced large-scale mutations, with juvenile mice displaying a signiﬁcant increase in RaDR foci across all timepoints, peaking at 3 months post-exposure (Fig. 4e). The decline in RaDR foci from 3 to 10 months likely reﬂects turnover of mutant cells or expansion of RaDR-positive regions. Even at 5 ppb NDMA, a small but signiﬁcant increase in RaDR foci was detected at 10 days post exposure in juvenile mice (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In contrast, adult mice displayed only a modest increase in recombination events, ﬁrst detectable at 3 months post-exposure and slightly elevated in longterm mice at 10-11 months post-exposure (Fig. 4e), potentially due to persistent low-level proliferation. The age-dependent discrepancy in NDMA-induced RaDR foci was also evident after intraperitoneal injection, with juveniles displaying an 11-fold increase compared to adults (Supplementary Fig. 1d), further reinforcing the heightened susceptibility of younger animals to NDMA-driven large-scale genomic alterations. Clonal expansion of mutant cells is a crucial step in tumorigenesis, where cells acquiring oncogenic mutations gain a selective advantage and proliferate44. This process allows the mutant cells to accumulate additional genetic and epigenetic alterations, ultimately contributing to the development and progression of cancer. We analyzed liver images from each timepoint for large RaDR foci representative of clonal expansion events8,45. Analysis of long-term mice at 10-11 months post exposure revealed a 5-fold increase in clonal expansion events in juveniles treated with NDMA compared to controls (Fig. 4f), an effect not observed in adults. The substantial increase in de novo mutagenesis and clonal expansion are consistent with early stages of tumor development. Duplex sequencing across a small fraction of the genome (48 kb of 20 endogenous genic and intergenic loci) provided a highly sensitive, quantitative mutagenicity readout and revealed pronounced, agedependent differences in NDMA-induced mutagenesis. Juvenile mice exhibited a dramatic ~186-fold increase in per-base mutation frequency (MFmin) compared to controls (Fig. 4g), while adults showed substantially lower levels (~51-fold, ~3.6-fold less than juveniles), reﬂecting the combined amplifying effects of juvenile proliferation and DNA repair deﬁciency2,6,46,47. NDMA-induced mutation spectra were dominated by GC →AT substitutions, with greater elevation in juveniles (Fig. 4h), and the overall signature primarily matched alkylation-associated COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer) SBS11 (Fig. 4i), conﬁrmed by high similarity to reconstructed proﬁles (Supplementary Fig. 5)6. Duplex sequencing also deﬁned clonal expansion quantitatively by calculating the ratio of MFmax (total mutations) to MFmin (unique mutations), which was markedly increased only in NDMA-treated juveniles (Fig. 4g), directly demonstrating clonal outgrowth of mutant hepatocytes. These mutational ﬁndings are consistent with the observed heightened gptΔ point mutations and clonal expansion of RaDR foci. The concordance across these methods emphasizes the mutational burden in juveniles, providing a mechanistic bridge between early mutagenesis and the later development of liver pathology and tumorigenesis after NDMA exposure.

Exposure age determines severity of liver pathology and cancer risk Results thus far demonstrate that DNA damage, inﬂammation, proliferation, and mutagenesis are more prominent in younger mice exposed to NDMA. For several endpoints, juvenile mice exhibited acute susceptibility, whereas adults appeared completely resistant. To investigate the long-term consequences of NDMA, we evaluated liver pathology 10-11 months post-exposure in Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice (Fig. 5a). Younger mice displayed signiﬁcant increases in hepatocellular hypertrophy, hyperplasia, and single-cell necrosis, all features less

pronounced in adults (Fig. 5b)14–16,24,48. Sustained inﬂammation, characterized by persistent immune cell inﬁltration, was observed exclusively in juvenile mice exposed to NDMA. These histopathological changes reﬂectpersistent, low-grade hepaticinﬂammation and cellular stress, accompanied by recurrent cycles of cell death and regeneration, processes known to drive liver cancer development14–16,49. In addition to local tissue damage, NDMA-induced hepatic pathology in juveniles manifested systemically. Notably, this weight loss developed later in life rather than acutely, likely reﬂecting progressive hepatic pathology rather than acute NDMA toxicity (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Consistent with hepatocellular hypertrophy, liver weight was signiﬁcantly increased only in NDMAtreated juvenile mice (Fig. 5c)50. In addition, lung weight was elevated in these animals, in line with the known metabolism of NDMA in pulmonary tissues (Supplementary Fig. 3d)2. Adult mice, however, did not display signiﬁcant changes in body or organ weights. The pronounced separation of these phenotypes between age groups likely underlies differences in cancer susceptibility. Pathological assessment revealed NDMA-treated juvenile mice harbored a signiﬁcantly higher incidence of tumors compared to both untreated controls and adults (Fig. 5d), with neoplasms identiﬁed in the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes (Supplementary Table 1). Liver tumors, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma, were most prevalent in younger mice exposed to NDMA, while none were observed in adults. The severity of liver tumorigenesis in juveniles is further illustrated by representative liver images and histopathology (Fig. 5e, f). Juvenile mice also displayed the highest frequency of NDMA-induced pulmonary adenomas (Supplementary Table 1). Remarkably, submandibular lymphoma was detected exclusively in NDMA-treated juveniles, representing a unique ﬁnding in this study2. These results demonstrate that the heightened susceptibility of younger mice to early genomic instability ultimately manifests as exacerbated liver pathology and increased cancer risk, persisting many months after NDMA exposure.

Sex modulates NDMA-induced DDR and mutagenesis in juvenile mice During the course of analyzing the susceptibility of juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice to NDMA, we observed notable sex-speciﬁc differences. Male mice exhibited a higher induction of NDMA-induced γH2AX compared to females (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b), despite equivalent levels of O6MeG and 3MeA DNA adducts (Supplementary Fig. 6c). As expected with hepatic injury, males showed a pronounced induction of proliferation markers (Ki67, PCNA, MCM2; Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Conversely, females demonstrated a more robust p21 (Cdkn1a) induction, as measured via RNA-seq (Fig. 6a) and immunoblotting (Fig. 6b), indicating enhanced cell cycle arrest. Consistent with their strong p21 induction, females did not upregulate proliferation markers following NDMA exposure (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b), reinforcing their reliance on cell cycle arrest over regenerative proliferation and potentially mitigating genotoxic stress. Sex markedly inﬂuenced NDMA’s carcinogenic potential in juvenile mice. Male mice exhibited elevated large-scale mutation (RaDR foci) burdens compared to females at all timepoints up to 10-11 months post-exposure, culminating in a 2-fold difference in long-term mutants (Fig. 6c). This sex disparity extended to the expansion of mutant cells, with clonal expansion events demonstrated only in males (Fig. 6d). Interestingly, point mutations were not signiﬁcantly altered by sex at 3 months post-exposure (Supplementary Fig. 6d). Pathological analysis

aligned with RaDR data, showing that males developed more NDMAinduced hepatocellular hyperplasia (Fig. 6e) and sustained greater weight loss than females (Fig. 6f). These ﬁndings underscore sex as a critical variable in NDMA risk assessment, with male predisposition linked to enhanced and more persistent liver pathologies.

Repair-proﬁcient mice display attenuated juvenile susceptibility While repair-deﬁcient Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice serve as a highly sensitive model, studies in WT mice revealed attenuated but mechanistically similar responses, highlighting both the relevance of NDMA exposure to the general population and the protective effects of functional repair pathways. As expected, the levels of NDMA-induced O6MeG and 3MeA in WT mice were greatly reduced compared to repair-deﬁcient counterparts (Fig. 7a vs. Fig. 1f). Nevertheless, unrepaired O6MeG adducts were signiﬁcantly elevated in both juvenile and adult WT mice, with levels comparable across age groups. Despite low adduct burdens, WT juveniles displayed a statistically signiﬁcant increase in γH2AX suggestive of residual replication stress and DSBs, an effect absent in adults (Fig. 7b, c). Transitioning to downstream effects, WT mice demonstrated mild transcriptomic changes in response to NDMA treatment; however, these changes closely resembled those in Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice, including upregulation of Mbl2 (inﬂammation) and Ephx1 (detoxiﬁcation), as well as a juvenile‑speciﬁc downregulation of Cyp2e1 (Supplementary Fig. 7a, b). Despite these subtle molecular changes, immuno- ﬂuorescence revealed an NDMA-induced proliferation (Ki67) increase in WT juveniles immediately post-exposure (Fig. 7d), which may promote replication-dependent mutagenesis. Indeed, RaDR foci were signiﬁcantly elevated in WT juveniles across all timepoints (Fig. 7e) but resolved faster than in repair-deﬁcient mice (Fig. 4e), with no clonal expansion events detected (Supplementary Fig. 7c). This demonstrates that WT levels of AAG and MGMT proteins limit mutant cell outgrowth despite initial mutation induction. In stark contrast to juveniles, WT adult mice showed no increase in NDMA-induced proliferation (Fig. 7d) or RaDR foci (Fig. 7e), further substantiating the role of age in mutagenic susceptibility. Long-term analysis revealed no histopathological changes in WT mice at 10-11 months post NDMA exposure (Supplementary Fig. 7d). Although NDMA-induced tumors were detected in long-term WT juveniles, the increase was not statistically signiﬁcant compared to adults, which exhibited no tumors (Supplementary Table 1). As expected, detecting subtle NDMA effects in WT mice requires larger cohorts compared to repair-deﬁcient models, reinforcing the utility of Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice for mechanistic studies. Collectively, these results demonstrate that NDMA inﬂicts measurable genomic stress, even in repair competent systems, so long as animals are young.

Discussion While prior studies have investigated the effects of NDMA on young animals, our study provides the ﬁrst in-depth, direct comparison with adults, thereby revealing the biological consequences of NDMA at an early stage of life2. The striking age-dependent differences in response to NDMA exposure highlight a synergistic interaction between developmental stage and environmental exposure. Juvenile Aag-/-;Mgmt-/-

mice, deﬁcient in the removal of NDMA-induced 3MeA and O6MeG, displayed markedly elevated levels of downstream DNA damage, inﬂammation, mutagenesis, and liver injury compared to their adult counterparts. These ﬁndings demonstrate the importance of age as a key factor when evaluating the toxicological impact of environmental contaminants, particularly nitrosamines. The dramatic differences between juvenile and adult responses challenge the adequacy of standard adult-centric toxicology testing. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Test Guideline 488 for mutagenicity evaluationpermits the use of younger animals(4-6 weeks old atthe start of treatment) for somatic tissue assessments when scientiﬁcally justiﬁed52. Our data provide clear scientiﬁc justiﬁcation: even in DNA repair-deﬁcient adults exposed to NDMA, downstream effects were substantially attenuated compared to juveniles, despite comparable DNA adduct levels across age groups in both WT and Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- mice. This clearly demonstrates that juveniles and adults differ fundamentally in their responses to DNA adducts, rather than in adduct formation or removal2,4,7. Given the pronounced differences between juvenile and adult outcomes extending beyond mutations to clonal expansion and tissue

pathology, our ﬁndings from mice younger than the standard guideline recommendations (3 weeks old at the start of treatment) suggest that even earlier exposure windows warrant investigation, and that standard uncertainty factors may underestimate risk for children exposed to NDMA and related nitrosamines53. To directly test the role of proliferation in NDMA susceptibility, we treated adult mice with T3 thyroid hormone, a known inducer of hepatocyte proliferation51. T3 treatment signiﬁcantly increased NDMAinduced γH2AX levels and γH2AX-Ki67 colocalization, demonstrating elevated genotoxicity in dividing cells. Furthermore, T3 exposure ampliﬁed the frequency of sequence rearrangement mutations in NDMA-treated adults, recapitulating juvenile vulnerability. The data support a replication-dependent model, wherein replication forks encountering DNA adducts generate genomic gaps and strand breaks. Therefore, the enhanced susceptibility of juvenile mice stems largely from their elevated hepatocyte proliferation rates, as compared to a disparity originating from traditional toxicokinetic or toxicodynamic differences. This proliferative state exacerbates mutagenesis through replication-driven mutation incorporation and hyperrecombination, effects further ampliﬁed by injury-induced regenerative responses unique to the juvenile liver4–7,14,43. While previous in vivo studies have demonstrated that adult rodents can be susceptible to NDMA-induced mutagenesis, substantial variability remains due to differences in study design and animal models2,9,46,54. In the present work, stringent multiple comparison corrections limited the number of endpoints reaching statistical signiﬁcance in adults. By prioritizing a conservative statistical analysis approach, the reliability of conclusions is strengthened, emphasizing that age is a key determinant of NDMA susceptibility. For these studies, we focused primarily on DNA repair-deﬁcient animals exposed to a relatively high dose of NDMA to minimize animal use while maximizing detection sensitivity. Although this approach limits direct environmental relevance, both MGMT and AAG exhibit wide interindividual variability, including naturally occurring variants with reduced repair capacity documented in human cancers, highlighting the importance of genetic diversity in toxicological studies and supporting the Aag-/-;Mgmt-/- model as a physiologically relevant system2,4,7. Comparable biological responses were observed in DNA repair-deﬁcient juveniles following both drinking water and intraperitoneal NDMA administration, showing that the route of exposure does not markedly inﬂuence hepatic outcomes. Even at a much lower, more environmentally relevant dose, we still detected a cellular stress response, demonstrating the heightened sensitivity of younger animals. In repair-proﬁcient WT mice, juveniles also exhibited NDMAinduced DNA damage, proliferation, and large-scale mutations, though at reduced levels, emphasizing the need for expanded WT studies with larger cohorts.
